your mind often, vowing never to be friendly witt. me again, but you could not help yourself. In spite I of your mind, your loving heart has been pre- dominant, and you have looked on me as more than a frierto sometimes. Haven't you, dearest ? j He spoke in soft, subdued tones. The effect of I his words was magical. In a moment the girl I softened towards him. _ _

"He is not all evil," she assured herself. "No man could speak such words with such fervour and be a scamp and reprobate." She would not be harsh and unkind to him, at any rate. He spoke again. "I am not perfect. I have done wrong. I have, in my blind, misguided infatuation, wronged you, Ella. But I have loved ru. I love you now, and you love me. I know it. Your lips say that you love another, but your heart declares that you love me. Why go out to far-off land to face danger, to face, maybe, mu/7 suffering and privation, to face war? Why g one who cannot love you more than I, who cannot love you as much as I love you? Why go to him? He is doubtless absorbed in his money-grabbing-- these gold miners think of little else but their gold. Why go to him? His heart may be as cold as his gold. Stay with me; my heart is warm, my love is hot! I think only of you. Naught else comes between me and my love for you. You are my sole thought! You are my life—my all! Stay with me, Ella; sweetest Ella, stay I" His impassioned speech thrilled the trembling girl. She quickened at his every word. Her heart leaped wildly within her. This was love! This was love

"Come, Ella!" the persuasive, coaxing voioe spoke again. "Come, Ella; come with me! You'll be mine. You are mine! Curse it! no man shall have you but I " She looked with alarm into his bloodshot eyes. His face was flushed with excitement, yet a look of gloating triumph was plainly written upon it. Intuitively she appiThended her imminent danger. His desperate words rang in her ears. "Oh, let me go. Let me go, Ralph—Mr. Cart- leigh. I don't know where I am! I'm ill. Let rae go I " He took her by the arm and led her from the park, and, entering a cab, they were soon conveyed to the town. At the door of her aunt's house she bade hir good-bye. He was returning to Dalesworth that night—Tuesday—and promised to visit her again at the week-end. "Ha! ha 1 " he cried, exultingly, as he was whirled homeward. "I've got her safe this time. A close shave, though. A deuced clogs shave! She was bent on going out to that one-time piecer, Steve the Outlander. Ha! ha! Our little melo- drama is becoming much mellower. The villain is most successful in his enterprises. He captures the heroine on the brink of matrimonial suicide. Really, I must congratulate myself. I ought to have been a playwright. I've an eye for dramatic effect—two eyes, in fact. Now for another plot. I must get hold of the rhino, and plenty of its, then I'll sport my darling heroine off to the Con- tinent. She is in want of a change, so am I; and after I have made my last haul, a change will, I reckon, be politic on my part."

div.head: LADIES' LETTER:II,
div.p: LADIES' LETTER:II,
MY DEAR. NELLIE,

I will briefly run through a few of the latest shapes in chapeaux I have recently noticed. One .I saw was a delightful toque of turquoise-blue glee& elaborately tucked all over. Another was an artistic hat of sage-green straw, trimmed with creamy guipure lace, shot peach-coloured glac‘ silk, and folds of green tulle. There are bows of silk on the left side, and sprays of very natural mauve lilac. Under the brim on the left side there are rosettes of green tulle and pale-coloured pansies, and the brim is lined with tucked green tulle. A very becoming hat was in black and white straw, trimmed with soft folds, and large rosettes of black tulle, whilst the lady's friend was wearing a smart toque, with a square crown of fancy straw, in the new blue, with a brim of finely- tucked chiffon. On the left aide there are several rosettes of narrow fancy straw, in a darker shade of blue, some blue wings, and clusters QI mauve and white hydrangeas.

Recent garments which I have seen show a new and very smart combination of the lighter-weight tweeds and the heaviest grass lawns. I will ask you to imagine a walking frock of bog-brown cloth made with a pinafore bolero, one of those boleros that cover the front of the bodice like a shield (fastening over on the shoulder and beneath the arms), stand out an inch or two from the figure, and end so far above the waist that the corselet can be seen beneath! The lawn, which should be just the colour of hay, a shade or two paler than the regulation khaki, plays the part of strappings, binding the pleats on the skirt neatly down' and on the bolero outlining the edges. The vest and corselet are also made of it, and should the picture fail to please, there might be substituted for the rich brown cloth a poplin gown, banded or piped with the finest linen, a union of fig-green and blue.

The blouse is changed in name, but just as popular as ever. It is now called "bodice," and is quite distinct from the skirt. Some of the newest have a very narrow basque, rounded at the sides and falling rather deeper in flat pleats at the back. A belt keeps the whole in position. The lace bodices are draped from a point on the right shoulder, and many of them have a jabot of edging lace following the line of draping.

le latest development of the rage for perpen- dicular tucks applies them to straight-backed little coats that have at last, begun to replace the warm and heavy winter garments. Some of them are made of poplin, and are tucked from the neck to a couple of inches below the waist, whore the fulness is released and allowed to flow out in a subdued sort of fulness similar to that on the dress skirts. Sometimes a simulated yoke bteaks the monotony of the straight lines. On the top of the sleeves the tucks arc carried down in lino with the yoke. The smartest race-coats are tucked from the waist to a depth of from a quarter to half a yard, the pleats being over an inch wide. The sleeves are tucked horizontally down their entire length. Very often the bodice is almost covered with a rich tr. uipure or gimp trimming,. and this may, or may not, be continued to the hem of the garment on eithe: side of the front. It makes a very handsome finish to a coat made of silk or khaki canvas over silk. This latter is to be a favourite combination for the coming season.

Batistes and er6pons will receive their due share of attention as the weeks wear on, but of our faithful friend, foulard, it is said we are beginning to tire. Whether in the fashion or out of it, foulard will always be worn to some extent, for its good wearing qualities and its smart appear- ance. Taffetas will be the material par excellence, but nowadays we wear our taffetas with a differ- ence. It is no longer the somewhat harsh un- pleasing substance considered gnod enough for skirt linings; the taffetas of to-day is supple and soft, and runs through the whole gamut of ex- quisite shades. Taffetas plain and ta.Tetas em- broidered; especially lovely is it in pure white or ivory, recalling a delicate piece of carving, or a specimen of old lace.
Your loving
J&NNIE,

div.head: "Lancashire Sketches," &c.
div.p: "Lancashire Sketches," &c.

CHAPTER XIX. Henry Cartleigh sailed for South Africa early in May. The scene of his future labours would be in the upper part of Natal, near the mighty Drackens.. burg Mountains, where, dotted about on the brown slopes and in the verdant valleys, were the sun- coloured huts and kraals of the Kaffirs, his black flock. , _ _

Ere he departed from Dalesworth the missionary had given as much of his spare cash as he could well spare to his spendthrift brother. "You had better spend a bit of the cash on this heathen," Ralph had said. "I'm as utterly lost as any of your interesting savages; but a little, ready money might enable me to find salvation again. I shall never find it in Dalesworth, that's a certainty; so, like yourself, I shall probably clear out to fresh fields and pastures new ere long.' • Henry never sermonised his brother; he knew how futile that would be; so, in his good heart, he cheerfully gave as much money as he could, expressing the hope that Ralph would find in the "new pastures" much success and more happiness. And so the brothers parted. Every week-end Ralph journeyed to Southport, and in promenading about the town visiting the theatres, in country drives, he revelled in Ella's

company. The girl was becoming dangerously attached to him again, and each day saw her more amenable to his influence. Her aunt, perceiving this, expostu- lated with her, and was pitilessly snubbed for her interference.

Ella was aware that the factory-master's son was not an ideal lover. His conduct at times was most reprehensible. He was quixotic, reckless, wild, prone to excessive drinking, a gambler, a profligate; yet with all these defects, there was an indefinable attraction about him.

As she compared him with quiet, steady, plodding Steve, as she knew him two years ago, the com- parison made her smile. They were as divergent as the poles in disposition. Steve appeared uninteresting, mediocre. Quiet, plodding fellows were well in their way; but the dashing, reckless, dare-devil cavaliers were always interesting and attractive, and were preferable. Here, then, was the secret of Ralph Cartleigh's power over her. He was polished in dress and manner; he had the bearing of a gentleman. "As a partner for life," reflected Ella, "the plodder, without doubt, is the better of the two. It would never do to marry a rake, a spendthrift, a drunkard." _

So, soberly and dispassionately considering the matter, she came to the conclusion that the safer course, though perhaps not the pleasantest, would be to throw over the rake and make sure of the plodder. A letter from Steve decided her. After referring to her mother's death and Ella's consequent lonely state, he proposed that the girl should join him in South Africa. They could be married in Capetown, then return to the Transvaal, and working together for a few years, they would prosper, and soon be enabled to revisit the Old Country again, and there spend their days ever afterwards in happiness and comfort. "A pretty picture," thought Ella. "For years I expect it would be very humdrum and monotonous, this working for a 'fortune.' Steve has already been out two years, and doesn't appear to have made much of a pile yet, or he would have sent me more than twenty-five pounds for my passage- money and wedding trotcsseau. Ah, well, I must make the best of it, I suppose. He says he is dying to see me. I'm afraid I shall be dying when I see him, dying at thought of the unromantic drudgery of scraping together a few pounds a month for several years. Perhaps, though, there will be some romance about life in these gold mining places. We shall see. At any rate, it will be a change, and, oh, I do hunger for a change of one kind or another 1" On a warm, sunny evening in June, 111 a was seated on a form in Hesketh Park, Southport. Ralph Cgirtleigh, cigar in mouth, was standing at her side, looking out across the miniature lake where, on, the far bank, the swans were trimming their feathers.

Ella had told him of— Steve's letter and her decision. He had listened to her quietly for a time, offering no observation whatsoever. At length, flinging his cigar stump into the lake, he seated himself close beside her, and, in a quiet, matter-of-fact tone, began: "So you prefer to be the wife of a gold miner then ? "
_ "Yes "—very softly. "Wife of Steve the Outlander, eh; ?" This was spoken with cutting sarcasm, as his lips curled in a hard smile. _

"Why do you call him by that name?" Ella asked, in a tone of mild resentment. "Well, I don't know, bttt it seems to fit him." "Don't sneer any more, please. We may as well part friends." "Oh, certainly," said Cartleigh, lightly, as he pulled out a fresh cigar and commenced smoking tt. "Yes, certainly; let us part as friends—if we are.to part at all." "We shall certainly part." "You have quite made up your mind?" "Quite. I shall sail for South Africa next week." "H'm!" - -

He puffed vigorously at the cigar, and in his pre-occupation neglected to knock off the ashes. The fine powder besprinkled his stylish pants. He pulled out his silk handkerchief, and carefully brushed every speck away; then, gazing out across the lake, as if he could perceive on its far shore the Dark Continent, he resumed: "You don't know much of South Africa ? " "I do not." "It is an unhealthy country." "Indeed? Someone I know says that it is most healthy." "He is a ii-" Cartleigh pulled himself up, and in a calmer voice said: 'I was about to say lie is liable, perhaps, to exaggerate the truth." "I believe Steve'? word," she said, stolidly.

"Oh, I doubt not," he rejoined, superciliously. "./ think, however, that he exaggerates the truth a little. South Africa is undoubtedly an unhealthy country." "Didn't you tell me that your brother was going out there for the benefit of his health ? "

"Partly that; but mission work is his chief con- sideration. I repeat, South Africa is an unhealthy country." "I am going out there, at any rate." "Yes, so I understand. Life in a mining city isn't usually very pleasant, and "—as a sudden inspiration came to him—" do you know that there is likely to be much trouble in Johannesburg before long ? ' "What do you mean ? " Her query betrayed some fear. The sly fellow was quick to note it. "I mean there is likely to be war there before "War?lon ' "

"Yes, war; bloody, cruel, horrible war! You have heard of the Outlanders? Ido not speak of an Outlander now," he added, meaningly. "These Outlanders are the miners and others in the Transvaal who are dissatisfied with the treatment they receive at the hands of the Boer Government —that is, the Transvaal Government. These Out- landers will fight—at least, some of them will— mark me, I do not say all; the Boers will fight against them. Our British Government will step in, then there'll be carnage and bloodshed with a vengeance. Do you see?" Ella clearly saw what he was leading up to. He wished to dissuade her from joining Steve. Was this true that he told her, or was it false? She had heard Ben, the warehouseman, speak of the oppressed Outlanders. Steve himself, too, had hinted at disaffection in the Golden City. She remembered the Jameson Raid. Perhaps it would all end as Ralph Cartleigh predicted. "So, you see, it won't be all plain sailing in the land of gold," he continued. You wouldn't like to be among the fighting, would you? And I'm sure someone else wouldn't, though, so far as he is concerned, I shouldn't trouble one way or the other, if I were you. Perhaps it will be as well if we resolve not to part, eh ? " "I shall go! I must go. I have made up my , mind to go," Ella replied. "Have you really and truly made up your mind to go ? " He knew what a fickle mind it was. Ella was a human weathercock, swayed by every breeze. "I have," she answered, decisively. He smiled in a doubting way. "Ah, I know that. mind. It is very tricky, very vacillating, very, ii very strange in its workings. You have made up 1

div.head: CTIAPTER XX.
div.p: CTIAPTER XX.

On the following morning Ralph Cartleigh lingered about his home longer than usual. He was accustomed to leave for the mill before nine o'clock, but at ten he was still roaming about, passing from the breakfast-room to the drawing- room, from thence into the hall. Once he entered the little sitting-room, where his father sat at his desk poring over figures; and so absorbed was the factory-master that he did not notice tilt, entrance and quick departure of his son. "Confound him! I wish he'd be off," Rah,* said, impatiently, as he turned into the con- servatory. "He's totting up his bank account, end reckoning.up every precious farthing, I'll swear, as if each one was worth a hundred pounds. have to reckon up more carefully after I've eashed my little cheque." He drew from his pocket several slips of paper, each containing the signature, "James Cartleigh." It was loose, sprawling handwriting, and not difficult to imitate. Ralph compared the slips with others bearing imitations in his own handwriting. "Can't tell one from the other," he observed, sotto voce. "Mine's exactly like the original—not a pin to choose between 'em. At any rate, the bank folks will pass mine, and I'll see that they pass a substantial amount of cash at the same time. I might as well be hung for a horse as sheep. Confound him 1 I wish he'd be quick ! If he sees me, he'll suspect I'm up to some game," Just then the sitting-room door closed with a bang, and the listener knew that his parent had left the apartment. As he hurried from the conser- vatory, Ralph saw his father pass down the gravelled walk and out of the garden-gate. The coast was now clear. His mother, sister, and the domestics were in another part of the house, and would not be likely to disturb him. He entered the room his father had just vacated, closed the door, and quietly turned the key in the •lock. He then walked over to the writing-desk which was open, and littered over with scraps ce.. paper. "justfas I thought," the young man remarked, taking up A. few of the slips which were scrawled over with figures. "He's been totting up a bit. He'll have to tot a lot down presently. Now, where's that cheque-book ? " He fumbled about amongst the books and loose papers, searched the pigeon-holes and the drawers— those that happened to be unlocked—but could not find the object of his search. "Foiled!" he ejaculated. "He must have taken it with him. Confound it! I'm done again!"

He threw down several loose papers he had taken up haphazard. "Ah What's this ?" he cried, as his eyes fell upon a coloured slip. He took it up. "Ah 1 A blank cheque! Blank—no; here's his signature, but no amount filled in Endorsed too! Egad 1 Just what I want I No need to forge his precious scrawl now. Ah, this is fine "he said, as he sat down and filled in the amount, words and figures —five hundred pounds. "The guv'nor's forgot to take this down to Meadstone. Well, never mind; I'll take the wage-money this week. I haven't been paid my wages lately. There!" as he care- fully blotted the cheque and placed it in his note- book, "I feel myself again. For a few weeks, at least, I shall be all right for spendin' brass.'" He left alp room as quietly as he had entered it, and, passing through the conservatory, slipped eAct. of the house unobserved. "Good-bye, mother. Good-bye to you all !" he said, pausing a moment ere he left the grounds. "I'm going for a merry holiday on the Continong. My conduct nearer home, at our watering resorts and other places, is objectionable to you. Igo for a time to more aristocratic but less frequented resorts, where my actions will not be so keenly observed. Ta, ta,!" .
He boarded a passing tramcar, and in a quarter of an hour was at Oldham. _

"I'll have a drink, to fortify myself," he said, as he entered his old haunt off Union-street. "Ah " he reflected, as he drank his liquor. "Reminds one of old times, when I squabbled here with Barrett over his miserable three hundred. " "And I paid him every cent; paid him with the money I annexed (politer term) from the cash-bag, and with the money brother Henry lent me. "But now there is real business toward. Bless me! I might just as well have made it a thousand as five hundred. Five hundred won't last long; but perhaps if I'd made it more the bank folks would have been suspicious. As it is, the amount isn't much above the usual weekly sum drawn for wages. Don't suppose they'll suspect anything by drawing it a couple of days beforehand. If they do ask questions I'll be ready for them." Arrived at the bank, he calmly handed the cheque over. The counter clerk who took it passed it on to the chief clerk, who, recognising Ralf.,* nodded familiarly. "How will you take it?" he asked. "As usual. Or, stay Give me the extra fifty in gold, please." The money was placed on the counter—a heavy pile. Then Ralph remembered he had nothing to carry it in. He had quite forgotten to bring? bag. He was equal to the emergency. "How thought- less of me," he said. "I've left the bag across the way. I called there for a drink. I'll be back in a minute."

He bolted out, and, recollecting that there was an outfitting establishment near by, he went to the place and purchased a small bag. "That's all right," he said, re-entering the bank premises with a smile, and quickly he deposited the cash in the bag and was away again. "I've two clear days before me before this will be found out," he said to himself. "I'll stay in Manchester to-night, and go to Southport to-morrow morning, when Miss Ella must accompany me to Paris without further delay." He spent the earlier hours of the evening at a Manchester rausic-hall, then later, in the privacy

of his room, he Indulged in a solitary carousal, priming himself with champagne. At, two o'clock in the morning the night-porter found him slumbering in his chair, and, with the assistance of a fellow-porter, put him in bed, where he lay until noon. His awakening was the signal for much noise and tumult. "Boots!" he yelled, as he caught sight of that unfortunate individual hurrying along the corridor. "Why didn't you waken me at eight o'clock, as I told you ? " "I tried, sir, but you wouldn't be wakened." The angry man swore savagely. "Call a cab! Fetch my bill! Take this luggage down!" he cried, imperiously. In ten minutia he was whirling along to the station in a hansom. "Curse my luck! Half the day gone! We ought to have been in London by this time."

He had to vtait half-an-hour for the Southport train, and spent the time in excitedly pacing the platform, glancing furtively about him continually. "Bahl I've nothing to fear!" he assured him • self, as for the twentieth time he glanced anxiove'r towards the station entrance. "It won't be fort., out until to-morrow, when Meadetone goes for the wage-money. And then—well, only a few of them will hear of it. The guv'nor will hush it up. He won't want the family name disgraced again. He'll keep mum. It's his own fault. He told me to clear out, but wouldn't give me anything to clear with. I'm merely taking travelling expenses." Though he tried to persuade himself he had nothing to trouble about, he was, nevertheless, uncommonly perturbed. He was a common thief, as low as the lowest, and meaner than most of the poor rascals who pilfered in the streets, for he had robbed his own father.

"Ah, well, bother it !" he cried, after much uneasy reflection. "I'll soon forget in happy enjoyment. It's a good job I've not got such a conscience as brother Harry." The train started at last, and about three o'clock he arrived in Southport. Hailing a cab, he drove at once to Ella's abode.

r.A. "You want Ella ? " said her aunt, in surprise, replying to Cartleigh's excited query. "Why, don't you know she has gone to South Africa ? " "Not gone, but going. She's going next week." "No, she's gone this week. She did intend to go next week, but suddenly made up her mind to go at once. She left here this morning, and sails to-morrow."

Ralph Cartleigh swore in his wrath. The astonished woman, who had scarcely under stood the .relations which had existed between thin man and her fickle niece, stared in amazement at this display of violent rage. "Didn't she write and tell you she was going ? " she asked, timidly. "No, curse her! She didn't," he retorted, and without another word stamped away. At the railway station he examined the time- tables carefully. "Oh, I'll manage it all right yet, Miss Flyaway," he said at length. "You've got a good start, but I'll pick you up at Southampton on Saturday. Meanwhile, I'll make preparations fore the South African trip. It's a little further than the Con- tinent, but that doesn't matter; perhaps it will in every way suit me better. We'll travel together, my girl, on the same boat, and if I don't capture you before the end of the voyage, I'll write myself down a Dutchman or a Boer."

He remained over night at Southport, and early on Friday morning took train for London. Having made sundry purchases in the metropolis, he proceeded to Southampton. That evening, as he walked down to the quay, he had the pleasure of seeing the Castle liner which had sailed from the Thames in the early hours of the morning drop anchor in Southampton Water. "When the mails go aboard to-morrow," he mused, "a male will go with them who will not be so easily despatched as the other mails. Ah what a splendid surprise it will be for Rayburn when she discovers that her Ralph aboard her Castle liner 1" Then his thoughts turned homeward.

"I wonder if the guv'nor will sleep as soundly !--9-aight as I shall? I guess he will be tearing Tuft hair now—what little he has left to tear. Poor old guv'nor, and poor, proud, haughty mother and sister I would fain have bid you au revoir, but 'twas not to be. For a time, at least, the black sheep of the flock will cease from troubling you I" On the following morning, as he sailed out to the big ship in the tender with several scores of emigrants, he was in exceptionally high spirits. The idea of exploring South Africa was positively exhilarating to him. "I shall be one of the wrong 'uns, " jie said." The country swarms with that class, I understand; men who leave their country for their country's good. I shall feel quite at home amongst. that class. And, in order to do the thing properly, like the rest, I'll live up to my new name." He had purchased a first-class ticket in the name of Ralph Percival, and as Mr. Ralph Percival he was entered on the list of passengers, which the chief steward held in his hand as he stood at the end of the gangway and awaited the new arrivals. As Percival walked up the gangway, he scanned the faces of those who peered over the bulwarks and rails of the big vessel, half-expecting to see Ella Rayburn. She was not within view, however. He was conducted to his cabin by a steward, who shouldered his large travelling-bag; another stewrz4 had come forward to take the smaller bag, bwa. Percival, thinking of the precious contents, thanked the man, and carried it himself. For the next few hours there was much stir and bustle aboard the Braemar Castle. It was not until late in the afternoon, after the last mails had been hauled aboard, that the hubbub ceased. Then through the placid water, glittering in the sunlight, the mighty vessel cleaved her way and bore Capewards. The passengers, having dined, swarmed on deck, and conversed with each, other, or quietly stood apart and gazed tearfullY landward. Ella Rayburn leant over the bulwarks and looked wistfully at the fast-receding shore, and her eyes were as moist afithe rest. She remembered that it was exactly two years since Steve had left England's shores; and now she realised what his feelings would then be on leaving the land of his birth. She thought with anguish of all that had passed in those two brief years—brief in time, yet protracted, long, weary years for her. She thought of her life in Dalesworth after Steve had gone, of her first lonely walk through Daisy Nook, when Ralph Cartleigh joined her. She trembled as she thought of the day-trip to Buxton, and her disgust with Cartleigh on that occasion. She thought of their reconciliation, of the Christ- mas Day episode when Cartleigh rescued her from drowning. She thought, too, of life at the mill, of cheery Ben's merry chat, the gossip at breakfast-time, the Wakes trip to Blackpool; she recollected tha7 week of rare, giddy delight. \ Then the Christra • ball rose before her, and she shuddered as Ole thought of its termination. Then came the time when she left the mill, roaming about seeking for work which could not be found. Then her mother's tragic death, leading up to the present time, when at the last moment, in fear and trembling, she had hurried away from Ralph Cartleigh. From beginning to end of these past two years, the factory-master's son stood out conspicuous. The musing girl perceived that he had been the central figure in her life, yea, in her whole thought. Little did she wot that the man of whom she thought was at that very moment contemplating her from the promenade-deck above. Hours afterwards, when she looked up at the star-lit sky and out on the dark ocean, that black figure stood gazing at her. For the two following days Ella scarce appeared on deck. Dread mal-de-iner held her in its grip, and only for a few moments did she venture to leave her cabin and seek the purer air on deck. When the Bay of Biscay was left behind, however, she, with most of the other women, came up from the stuffy cabin, and rejoiced in the pure, refresh- ing breeze which swept over all. She was yet faint and languid, and appeared to be in need of good nourishment. On the afternoon of the third day she was reclining in a camp-chair gazing listlessly out o'er the waste of waters. The other third-class pas. sengers—men and boys—were playing various dent, games, and making considerable noise thereby. Several of the women were sewing; some—of the foreign contingent—were combing and dressing the hair of the young children. Next to Ella sat a young mother nursing a month-old child, a puny, frail atom of humanity, which spent the greater part of its days and nights in pitiful wailing. The child's continual crying and the noise made by the boisterous men and lads about her, dis- tressed Ella greatly 7 Wearily she rose from her seat at last, and, walking towards the forecastle, sought for a quieter place. This part of the ship was more crowded and equally noisy, so she had perforce to return to her old place or go down into the cabin, where the heat was intolerable. She dropped into the camp-chair, and glanced half- reprovingly, half-pityingly at the poor, harassed mother, who dandled the squalling babe about in all positions in a vain attempt to quieten it. Then, as the din and clamour continued, the despairing girl buried her face in her hands. Her

div.head: "WOMEN'S CHAT."
div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

The National Bazaar at the Albert Hall in aid of the War funds, will be one of the principal events of the London season this year. The Committee earnestly appeal for contributions, whether in money or in kind, for the equipment of the seventy stalls which will be arranged to represent all the regiments at the front. The promoters hope to raise £50,000 to present to the. Queen, as trustee, for the sufferers by the war, and they have issued a pretty, and well executed badge, which it is hoped will become a popular decoration with the pub. lic on the occasion of the Queen's birthday. It only costs sixpence, and if everyone, who could afford that sum would devote so much to the purchase of a badge, the success of the bazaar would be more than assured. , The boast of the Boers that they would retake Bloem- fontein has not deterred Lady Robert's and her daughters from proceeding to the Free State capital. Lord Roberts evidently never bad any apprehension as to the renewed activity of the Boers, and one can quite understand that Lady Roberts met with an enthusiastic reception in Bloemfontein. That little town, though surrounded on all sides by the grim realities of war, is never likely to have such a gay aud busy time as it bee had during the six weeks or more, that the troops have been waiting there completing preparations. Military officers who have perfoice remained at home.are much:like the lonely ' sparrow on the housetop. They complain of empty dubs aud dull times, whilst half the aristocratic families of this country hate been represented in the Free State capital. The employment of homes in warfare inflicts untold suffering upon dumb animals,and it was one of the futile proposals at the Peace Conference at the Hague, that their use on the field of battle should be abolished. It is ro be feared that the suggestion is further from realisation than ever, for if there is one thing more than another which the war in South Africa has proved, it is that the advantage rests with the mounted force. Then in the Continental armies, not only are they em- ploying horses in greater numbers than ever but they are also training dogs, to carry messages on the battle field, to attack the enemy's cyclists, and render other services in warfare. There is also in addition to the dogs of war, the " Red Cross" dog, which is trained to minister to th 3 wounded. The dog carries saddle-bags, in which are a flask of brandy water, bandages' and so on, and it is taught to seek out the fallen and to lie down so that the wounded man may help himself. War it is true, is horrible enough without bringing dogs into it, but there have, nevertheless, been nuMberless cases, in which cur wounded soldiers have been lying out in the open for hours, before the ambulance could reach them, and to whom the "Red Cross "dog would have proved a bless- ing had it been at hand. The King of Sweden, who, accompanied by Queen Sophia, and the Crown Priecess Louise, is paying a long visit to this country, is the great grandson of Nanoleon'a famous General Bernadotte, and was born in 1829. He is therefore ten years younger than our Queen. On the death of his brother, he succeeded—in 1872—t0 the Throne, and in spite of the cares of State, his Majesty has found time for the exercise of considerable literary talent. In this respect King Oscar is easily first among the Sovereigns of Europe. Be has translated Goethe's " Faust " into Swedish, and is also the author of " A Memoir of Charles X 11.," and several publications under the nom de plume of Oscar Frederick. Queen Sophia of Sweden is a sister of the Grand Duke Adolphus of Lux- emburg, an aunt of the clever and accomplished Queen of Roumania, and also the Duchew, of Albany. The Baroness Burdett-Ceutte, who has just entered upon her eighty-sixth year, has been staying during the spring at San Remo. When but 22 years of age she in- herited from her grandfather. Mr Couttsi the fortune of nearly £2,000,000, the greater part of which she leas devoted to her long-life work of helping the poor, and afflicted. For half a century there has hardly been any great scheme of benevolence for which her help has not been forthcoming, though it has been the east end and poorer parts of the Metropolis that have mostly benefited by her numberless works of charity. It is nearly twenty years ago since the It,roness married Mr William Ashmead-Bartlett. That event took place when the Baroness was sixty-seven years of age, and Mr. Bartlett who was born in America, thirty. The death of Lord Londesbnrengh recalls the fact that it was while the Prince of Wales was on a visit to him at Scarborough, that His Royal Highness caught the typhoid illness, that as nearly cost him his life in 1871. The Prince was accompanied by the Princess of Wales who took no harm, but three weeks afterwards His Royal Highness was down with the fever,as was also his fellow guest, Lord Chesterfield. It was afterwards dis- covered that the sanitary arrangements at Lord Lonrho- boroughs were defective, and needless to say the occur- rence occasioned the greatest grief to the popular land- owner, who was so well known in Yorkshire. Narrow black velvet ribbon is employed by the mile jut ROW by all leading dressmakers, and promises to enjoy, if such a thing be possible, a. still wider vogue, as summer advances, and dainty muslin gowns become the general wear. We seem to have quite come to the conclusion that a very hot season lies before us, for most of the matins in preparation are being built wish transparent yolks and sleeves. This mode lacks much in the way of common sense. In the first place the risk is considerable, taking into consideration our very variable climate, and in the mond, it spells ruination to 0/lesi neck and arms. It is very easy to distinguish—vben in evening dress—the women who habitually, in hot weather,don a day blouse or bodice, of this discription. They are brenzed and freckled' to a degree. - _ .

White promises to be more worn than ever. By the vast numbers in mourning it will be widely patronised the pure" desd "white, permissible in mourning wear. To the complrxion, it is trying of course, but under the circumstances, this can not be avoided. Those whole choice is—happily—in no way restricted, will indulge in the ivory or cream white. The majority of complexions will stand these tints, and far from proving unbecoming, white is, generally speaking, particu!arly fascinating wear. The friends of the temperance movement will be mere than usually active this summer. The World's Temper- ance Congress will begin in London on June 11th at which it is expected Mr. T. W. Russell will preside. It is understocd that the Archbishop of Canterbury will take the chair at one of the ratherings. There will also be the mew century loaner of the National Temperance League, vrbieb the Marchioness of Lorne, Duchess of Argyll, is to open on the 12th of June. Among others taking a prominent pert is this affair, are the DuchesE. of Somerset, the Dowager Countess of Ecroll, the Bon. Mrs, Eliot Yorke, Miss Ellen Orme, who is the honorary seeretary, and the Hon. Mrs. Conrad Dillon. " MADGE."

thoughts at that moment *ere esptcusayglooflhl The voyage, so far, had been anything but delight- ful ; she looked forward with dismay to the flat fortnight she would have to spend in this part of the ship. The women, as a whole, were kind and helpful to her; they tried to make each other's lot as pleasant and comfortable as possible. The men and youths, too, in the main, were civil and con-, siderate. Some If them, however, boll, impudent fellows, seeing a young, good-looking girl along and unprotected, did not hesitate to pester and annoy her with their attentions. These fellows and the many dirty Jews who swarmed about were inesi repugnant to the timid girl. As she thought of what she would have to endurt during the remainder of the voyage, she lost heart and broke down completely, sobbing distractedly. The women regarded her with pity and cow miseration. "Poor lass!" observed one. "She feels lonelY, and no wonder, being all alone. It's bad enough for us that have our chaps and children about as. What must it be for her ? " Ella overheard this remark, and it evoked a fresh flow of tears. _ _
Then wiift" a start, she raised her streaming fac° as a hand was placed on her shoulder, and familiar voice spoke.

"Ella 1" She rose to her feet with a startled cry, theor overcome by the shock, staggered 'helplessly, aini would have fallen had not Ralph Cartleigh's arra borne har up. • Gently he led her into the after part of the ship; In the cosy, elegant saloon, where none invadeu their privacy, they sat, and when Ella had recovered from her surprise and realised that this was really' Ralph Cartleigh who sat beside her, she spoko collectedly and calmly. "What brings you here ? " ! "Why, what, indeed, but yourself ? " he replied. Then he told of his visit to Southport, spoke of his chagrin when he discovered that she had left him and once again declared his love and devotioa to her.

"But what are you doing in that part of 00 ship?" he asked. "I couldn't afford to travel saloon or second," she said, in apologetic tone, as if thorough', ashamed to make the admission. "I should have preferred to travel second-class, but-" "I see 1" he added, significantly. "Well, 111 soon have that altered." .
"What do you mean?" Ella asked, as he rose to his feet.
"I mean that I shall have you transferred to thig part of the ship." "What! No, you mustn't do any such thing, Mr. Cart-"

"S -s-s-h I My name is Percival, now. IC° protestations. It is useless." "But I shall not travel first-class." "Do you prefer second-class; then ? " "No, neither. I shall travel third-class:as I ero now doing." "Stop here a moment, please." He went away, and returned in a few moment with a triumphant smile on his face. "It's all right," he said. "I have seen the purser and the chief steward. The stewardess has gone for your things. Your cabin is No. 39." There was something so masterful about his con" duct that she felt it useless to resist. "I'm ashamed, Mr. Cart—Percival," she said, and her blushing face plainly betrayed her feeling. - "But all the same you are secretly glad," he rejoined. "You know that you will be more cora" fortable in your new quarters, will have better accommodation, better food, better attendance, and better society. Oh, I've been watching you these many days. I've seen that little solitary weeping figure, lonely and unhappy, seeking in vain for 5 friend amongst that tatterdemalian horde ef steerage passengers, that hotch-potch crowd of dirty' foreigners—and--poor Britishers." "Many of the people were kind and friendly', she said, feeling that he was unjust in his barer' references to her late associates. r "Oh, yes," he said, sarcastically. "Many of the men were kin's!' and—friendly to you, I noticed., The beasts! had difficulty in holding myself /0 check when I saw those leering, sensuous rascal° ogling you as they talked their filth." ; "They never talked filth to me. I would net allow them. At least, I would not stop Uto hear them." "Ah, well, we'll not quarrel over that. You ere well away from them now; and for the rest of the voyage you will be under my care. Won't that be jolly ? " , Very soon Ella was quick to discern how? gru was the change from the third to the first-cla, and she was appreciably grateful for her change of condition. Here there was plenty of room to move about; it was quieter and pleasanter in every way. There were luxurious rooms to lounge in, superb saloons to dine in, and cheerful, cool cabins t° sleep in. Chairs and settees in abundance were placed on the spacious promenade-deck, which we° never overcrowded with passengers, as was the forecastle-deck. "We're mostly millionaires in our part of the ship," said Ralph. "The poor devils you Uwere among are would-be millionaires. There's the difference. The second-class are the go-between°, —the middlemen; or the middling men, I shoulo term them. Some of them are quite indifferent to money. There's Barnard, that tall, spiny fellotr with the serious white face. He's a consumptive, Isn't great on wealth; health he prizes roore, Poor devil! he's got much of one but little of the other. He's a good-natured fool, too; go,.aee amongst the poor beg„,,..ars in the steerage, tel"' with '(m, and gives them money. One of those cranks,, you know, always looking after other folla instead of himself. I believe he'd give the shi° off his back if he saw another poor chap goil without one. A conspicuous fool! He's discovere' another consumptive in the third-class, a lungleee fellow who was crowded in a cabin with five other men. Think of it, this hot weather! Ugh! coughed throughout the night, and the other fellows couldn't sleep, and, of course, he'd ne comfort, so Barnard gave the steward a sovereie, to put him in a cabin by himself. That's a fact one of the fellows who slept with the consumptive..., told me. That's the sort of fool Barnard is. he goes on throwing his sovereigns about in the° fashion, he'll most likely have to travel third' class himself before long. (7o be continued.)

div.head: BRITISH AND THEIR OMTICS.
div.p: THE BRITISH AND THEIR OMTICS.
(BY MR, H. %TRITIUM )

One thing that has struck tiar_4 very forcibly since I left Warrington twclve years ago, is the promin- ent and rather peculiar position Great Britain holds in the minds of other nations. I say of other nations because I am in the tothit of meeting, day by day, with workmen from nearly every clime. For in- stance, I am now working inclose relationship with two men, one a Frenchmen, and the other a Portu- guese Brazilian. Their talk, and the Cpler3tiol:lB they put to me about Eng Jana are simply amazing. That it is but a little speck on the map astonishes them, that it makes sucti a noise in the world astonishes them mire, and that it does all its work without conscription relying solely on its volunteers,strikes them as wonderful. _ _ _ _

At rare intervals I go into the city and mix with the crowds around the bulletin. The subject of discussion is always the same, viz. England and her doings. The listener is sure to hear that Eng- land is never victorious when she fights with white men. Her victories are always gained when fighing with the naked savage. "See how we beat her during the Rebellion, and again in 1812." The Scandinavian, the Frenchman, the German, and the Russian, so far as they can voice their opinions, will sing the same s.cing. The man in the street, to lump them up together, seems to be unaw are of the fact that German mercenaries were hired end paid by British gold, and by a German- British King to fight British rebels. They seem to Ise unaware of the fact that in 1812 England was preparing for the most glorious work a nation ever entered into. To save Europe from the greed and ambition of the "Little Corporal" was a mighty work for the tight little island, but it was accomp- lished.• To )'ear the street spouter, and to read the "Western Press "or the "European Continental Press," one would think that the doings of the Ger- mans and French in Africa, were just sublime, and ttiat Russia's doings in Finland were nothing lass than Godlike, and that while " Peace reigns in War- saw?' we are all to bend the knee and thank God we have such a Czar of all the Russias to fake. Peace Conventions.

I fear it is a fact that lam becoming more and more a hater of the Democratic mob. This does not mean that I could ever rest in the conservatise ranks The mobs in each party are as nearly alike as two peas. In saying this I am not referring so much to England as to America, yet in the two countries mob-voting is a Mistake. Let us get to higher ground.. I have just reed J. L. Wanklyn's article in the "New York fribune." It is the most masterly article I have read on the South African War. In answering Mr. Bryce's article condemning the action taken by the British Government, Mr. Wanklyn (A Yorkshire M.P. by the way), has done a great service. All who read his historical sketch will know a great deal of whet before they had no knowledge. My morning paper has just come in and I find in very large type the caption British walk into a Boer trap." This seems very strange, and after General Buller'a anxious inquiry whether British officers will ever learn the value of scouting, must emphaeize the spreading belief that British efficers are fit only to be led. The courage they have in .plenty, but not that military skill which saves life, and brings victory. That Colonel Bread wood should deliberately walk into ambush within twenty miles of Bloemfontein is really un- accountable. I see from a number of Canadian papers that a large correspondence is going on, showing a want of faith in British officers. This feeling is well illustrated in the case of the Duke of Norfolk. Red tape at the Post-office has driven him to the war, where in turn, he will meet with, and may chance to suffer through the red tape of the War-office. In connection with the ideas thrown out by the man in the street is the know- ledge that the man in the study does more,and again, says something worth listening to. From the study we may receive the lasinwe may also receive a little soothing anointment. iThen one is away from home it is always interesting to know what those around you think of your kin. During ller Majeaty'e reign England has played an important part in the world's affairs. While her people, (the mob I am not in love with) have fought for and gained liberty in a measure for themselves, they have been too often a little blind to the rights of others. Emerson tells us that England is the best of actual nations. Yet she sanctioned the partition of Poland, and betrayed Sieily,Greece,and Hungary. Speaking im 1817 at a meeting in Manchester he said some things that should have some point just now. I say this because I believe that the war in South Africa is not over, or nearly over. Mr. Emerson said : "And so, Gentlemen, I feel in re- gard to this age 4 England, with the possessiens, honours, and trophies, and also with the infirmities of a thousand years gathering around her,irretrie‘ - ably committed as she is now to many old Customs which cannot be suddenly changed; prassed upon by the transitions of trade, and new and all incalculable modes, fabrics, arts, machines, and competing population, I see her not dispirited, not weak, but well remembering that she has seen dark days before; indeed with a kind of instinct that she sees a little better on a cloudy els.y,and that in storm of battle and calamity she has a secret vigour and a pulso like a cannon. I see her in her old age, not decrepit, but young and still daring to believe in her powers of endurance and expansion. Seeing this I say, All Hail! mother of nations, mother of heroes, with strength still Equal to the time ; still wise to entertain and owift to execute the policy which the mind and heart re- quire in the present hour." This was said in 1847. It applies to-day with increased force, but if I may say to, or if I am able to read the signs of the times, the time is nigh when all the walls of caste must be broken down and capability in whatsoever sphere it may be found, must be hewn:: by the glnd hand to rine uo and do -its share of the world's work. April 2nd, 1900.
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

ST. PAUL'S SALE OF WORK.

In aid of various funds eonnected with St. Paul's Church, Warrington, the annual sale of work was held in the Infant',' School, Kendrick-street on Monday afternoon and evening. At che opening ceremony the Vicar (the Rev E R Tarbuck) predded, and the attendance inctud,d M'3 Beamont (who opened the sale) Miss Snith, the R,V9 EC E Carleton, H V Pigot, W Bracecamp, and J H Gr Hollingworth, Mrs Hooerts (the Mayoress), Mr e J C Parr, Mrs Peter Ryland, Mrs Smethurst, Mrs Edwin Smith, Miss Hsrrison, the Misses Owen, Mr R J Chorley (people's warden), Messrs J H Smethurst, A Burgess and Charles Hamilton (sidesmen), Dr Smith and Dr Adamq.

Tire Vican: in the course of his openieg remarks, stared that at last year's sia'.e they took a net sum of £l7l, and it was diviied int) the followiag sums : Mission lady's salary, £52 ; subscription to trio assistant clergy fund, £5O; All Saki& trial, £l2 ; day schools, £lO ; mothers' meeting £4 ; Girls Friendly Society sewing class, £2 ; flowers. &1., for the church, £3 ; cnuronwardens' acceunt, £l3 ; reserve fund for sewing material, £24. Toeir present needs were greater than last year. They required a second curate, and the amount given from the sale of work was only about a third of the present curate's stipend. It was to be hoped, therefore,that if possible more even than last year might be obtained. He had been delighted with the hearty co- operation of all the workers in the parish since he came. They were very glad indeed to see present so many staunch friends from outside the parisb. As they knew, theirs was not only a poor parish but was becoming poorer if possible every year, They absolutely depended for their very life upon the result of the sale, and there- fore upon the hearty support of those generous people who came out of their interest for the pari.h regularly to support them. Oa this occasion thsre was one lady present who would give them her blessing as she always had done. Mrs. Beamont was well known throughout the town aud district as a lady remarkable for her chari- table deeds and for her general kindly disposition. Her husband's name was revered by every Warring- tonian because his whole life seemed to have been de- voted to the service of other people. That she had con- tinued his good work was well-known. Sue was his (Mr. Tarbuck's) patron practically in the offering to him of the living of St. Paul's. It was well-known to Mr. Robert Davies that it was a fact that though the living was under trustees it was owing to Mrs.Beamont's championship wi'h Mr. Gibson Smith to urge her that the living was offered to him (Mr.Tarbuck). Mr. Davies vers kindly performed the opening csremony last year, and it was only fitting that Mrs. Beament should open the sale this year. He was sorry Mr. Davies was unable to be present. fie was not seriously ill now, but had only just recovered from an attack of influenza and would have to keep to the house a little longer. He wrote re- gretting his absence and wishing them a prosperous and successful afternoon. (Applause.) Mrs. BELMONT in opening the sale wished to say how very pleased she had been with the kindly and loyal way in which they had supported Mr. and Mra. T.rbuck in their excellent work ever since they came there. She hoped the sale of work would be even more successful than in previous years, and she had great pleasure in de- claring it open. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. .Beamout and said the name of Beamont was a household word in Warrington, and perhaps no name was more associated with the building of schools and religious and charitable work generally. Mr. CHORLEY seconded, and the vote was heartily carried. _ _ _

_ The business of the day was then proceeded with. The stalls were laden with useful and fancy articles. Throughout the day there was a good attendance and in the evening tbe room was crowded. The stalls and stallbolders were as follows :—No 1, Mrs Gibson Smith, Mrs Chorley, Mrs Lord, Mrs Bucb ton, ATM Laird, and Miss Reid ; No. 2, , the Misses Geddes and the Misses Hepherd ; No. 3, Mrs James Ricnardson the Misses Richards, and Mrs Fanshaw ; No. 4, the Misses Finney, Mrs Clarke and Mrs Parker ; No. 5, Mrs Tarbuck, Mrs James Lawton, Miss Theakstone, Mrs Chantry, Mrs Bridge, Mrs J H Smethurst, and Mrs Lindley ; No. 6 Mrs Hankinson, Miss Lythgoe, Miss Craik and Miss Ashurst; flower stall, Miss Rithbone and Miss Wainwright ; refreshment stall, Miss Westwell, Miss Brand, Miss fhtighton. Miss Ada Smethurst, Miss L'zzin Pickton. Miss May Meadows end Miss Riding (London); Working- stall, the Vicar, Mr C Hamilton, Mrs Fred Parsonage, Miss Snelson, Miss Emi:y Snelson,Miss Annie Powell and Mrs T Locker ; bran pie, Miss Gladys Hankinson, Miss Jane Chantry, and Miss Gertrude Warburton. The amount realised was £l2O.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
REV. R. J. CAMPBELL, 8.A., IN SOUTH AFRICA.

The distinguished young minister of Brighton has taken Cape Colony by storm by his eloquence and religious philosophic spirit. This is the testimony of a trustworthy man on the spot. Mr. Campbell gave an address to the Guild of the Loyal Women of South Africa, I whose objects are to cultivate kindly feeling and, goodwill among all residents in South Africa of whatever race or birth. Among his audience were H.R.H. Prince Eugene of Teck, Lady Edward Cecil, Lady Charles Bentinck, Mrs. Hanbury Williams, the Hon. Arthur Stanley (son of Lord Derby), and Sir Pieter Faure. • Everywhere Mr. Campbell is having crowded audiences and ministers at Kimberley, Durban, and Port Elizabeth have asked him to
visit these places. Mr. Campbell has met the principal residents of Cape Town including the Prime Minister, Mr. Rose-Innes, and Sir Gordon Sprigg.

div.head: OPEN-AIR PREACHING.
div.p: OPEN-AIR PREACHING.

The Free Church Chronicle for May has an interesting article on open-air preaching. The writer says that all efforts to reach the work- ing classes will be only very partially success- ful unless many more open-air services are held, and unless the services are greatly im- proved. "It is undeniable, we think, that open- air work has too much fallen into the hands of unlearned and sometimes rather narrow men. This explains why open-air preaching has rather come into discredit. It is a mistake, we are sure, to suppose that poor, unlearned men listen most eagerly to preachers whose worldly and intellectual status is the same as their own. There is no evangelical preacher in England too great and clever for an audience of English artisans." The writer suggests that there should be a Free Church Field Preaching Sunday once or twice every summer.

div.head: LORD NELSON'S DELUSIONS.
div.p: LORD NELSON'S DELUSIONS.

Lord Nelson, of Christian reunion fame, has made some extraordinary statements in Church Bells. He has got bold of the extraordinary and linaccountable idea that the Free Church Girls' Guild is an apeing of Churchmen, and, further, that some Free Churchmen propose to do away with sermons to make way for hymns and ornate services. Does Lord Nelson live in a balloon? The fact is, of course, that the Guild is being established to counteract (not to emulate) the proselytising activity of the Girls' Friendly Society. As for doing away with sermons to make way for hymns and ornate services, we suppose Lord Nelson remembers in a hazy sort of way that Dr. Barrett, at the Sheffield meet- ings of the National Council, pleaded for more outward charm, reverence, dignity, and beauty in worship. But no one would be more amazed than Dr. Barrett to hear that he wanted to do away with preaching.

div.head: MAY MEETINGS.
div.p: THE MAY MEETINGS.

The May meetings are on us now. There is nothing calling for speciiil remark on the agenda of the Free Church assemblies. The Rev. W. Cuff, of Shoreditch, succeeds Dr. Clifford in the chair of the Baptist Union—no two men could afford a more striking contrast. Mr. Cuff was trained at the Pastors' College, under Mr. Spurgeon, and he adheres to the theological views which the pastor of the Metropoiitan Tabernacle used to proclaim witk so much vigour. The address of Mr. J. Carrell Williams, M.P., from the chair of the Congrega- tional Union, is looked forward to with great interest. It will be the duty of the Union to appoint the Chairman for 1901. Already a number of names have been suggested; but there is no clear indication at present as to who is the favourite.

div.head: MR. PRICE HUGHES'S NEW COLLEAGUE.
div.p: MR. PRICE HUGHES'S NEW COLLEAGUE.

The Rev. Mark Guy Pearse desires to spend some months in travel, and in order that he may do this with an easier mind, arrangements have been made for giving Mr. Hughes a new colleague. The choice has fallen upon the Rev. J. Gregory Mantle, who has done a great work in Brighton, and has shown himself able to gather and handle large audiences. Mr. Mantle has been a successful missioner, and has promised to take part in the great united simultaneous mission to be held early next year. It is not to be understood that the partnership between Mr. Hughes and Mr. Mark Guy Pearse is dissolved. Mr. Pearse is still a minister of -the West London Mission, and hopes to be so as long as he lives.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL EXPERIMENT.
div.p: A SUCCESSFUL EXPERIMENT.

The unsectarian school founded by the St. James's Education League, Northampton, in opposition to the Church schools of the district, is enjoying gratifying success. It was opened fifteen months ago, and there are now 150 children in attendance. The total income of the Church schools last year was £1583, and the total voluntary subscriptions amounted to a little over £34! The public has no voice what- ever in tho expenditure of this £l5OO of public money. A number of Free Church Councils have taken in handthe provision of unsectarian elementary education in districts where there are only voluntary schools and no chance of a School Board. At Trowbridge, for example, a scheme involving the expenditure of nearly £BOOO, is in a fair way towards completion.

div.head: MARRIAGE LAW VAGARY.
div.p: MARRIAGE LAW VAGARY.

The Vicar of Tydd St. Mary, Lincolnshire, refused to marry a couple because the Noncon- formist bridegroom had not been baptized. Had he the law on his side? The point should certainly be cleared up. Because the Rector of the neighbouring parish of Tydd St. Giles made no demur to performing the ceremony. The Rev. Gordon Woodo.ate not only himself officiated, but his wife played the " Wedding March." This is a very pleasant conclusion. Has an incumbent the right to forbid a mar- riage because one of the contracting parties offends his orthodox susceptibilities?

div.head: GLASGOW EVANGELISTIC CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE GLASGOW EVANGELISTIC CAMPAIGN.

The six months' evangelistic campaign in the second city of the United Kingdom is now over. The results among children have been particu- larly cheering. Eight or ten quiet meetings were concluaecl every evening for boys and girls. Audiences of one thousand and over were the rule, and in more than one mission two services had to be held each night —one for those under 12 at 5.30 and a second for those over 12 at seven o'clock, or the first service for girls only and the second for boys only. More than 20,000 young people, without undue pressure, waited to after meetings, o.nd were personally spoken to and are row being individually followed by Christian friends in their own congregations, or by others where they have had no church connection. The pre- parations for the great mission organised by the National Free Church Council are being care- fully considered.

The sudden departure of the Rev. J. J. Langhans, 'ILA., from Padgate, where he has been vicar for many years has been a topic freely commented upon in the district during the past few days. There have been many rumours respecting the cause of Mr bangham's disappearance but we have no desire to give publicity to them. At the annual Eater vestry meeting held in the Padgete Church Institute,last Thursday evening,'the Rcter of War- riugton presided, and with great tact performed the difficult task of instructing the parishioners as to what they should do in the present emergency. div.head: APPLE DUMPLINGS AND SO ON.
div.p: APPLE DUMPLINGS AND SO ON.

"The man who refuses to eat apple dumplings cannot have a pure mind." So declared a famous vPgetarian a century ago. He had a horror of most meat dishes, especially of minced veal. Perhaps somebody who reads this lit-le lecture may he able to tell me whether apple dumplings have not largely gone out of fashion in England. If so, it is a pity, for they are good food when light ; but they are starchy, all the same, and demand a healthy and vigorous digestion. Therefore, even at the risk of being suspected of imp ure mindedness, the majority will have to say " No " to the average apple dumpling. Ah,dear me! It is the doctors and physiologists who say that the British stomach is no longer the mighty and fearless machine it was in the days of our grand- fathers and their fathers. We have a bigger and more dangerous navy, it is trn., but in good Booth, nay dys- peptic friends, a stomach that is able to dissolve a hard- boiled dumpling without a pang, is a better bulwark to the nation than monstrous guns and walls of steel. r The patriots who talk like this man, are they not legion ? " Ask yourself the question," as the Deal boatman put it. He says, as does Mr. Thomas White, of Oadby, that after every morsel he ate there arose great pain in his chest and stomach. In Oatober, 1891, he was seized with rheumatism, and confined to his bed sixteen weeks straight away. He couldn't move hand or foot, or bear to be touched ,he says ; and for six years following he remained in a pitiable condition—too weak to work and too wretched to care much what became of him.

Then a brother-in-law, Charles Norman, who had been cured of chronic indigestion by Mother Seigel's Syrup, told Mr. White that he believed it would also cure rheumatism, as he had learned that the one was the ause of the other. It, was an Humiliating idea, and Mr. White acted on it. "tater using this remedy for a week," he says, "I waa decidedly better. Presently I c ()old eat well, and all food agreed with me. The rheumatism disappeared root and branch, and I got back to my work strong and well; and up to this date I have had no illness, either dyspepsia et rheumatism. It is my opinion that by using Mother Seigel's Syrup a I man may safely eat whatever he likes and stand no chance of harm." Thomas White, London-road, Oadby, Inear Leicester, July 18th, 1899.

Hardly a doubt oft. The history of Mother Seigel's Syrup for 30 year; is in the box to testify to it. Disease succumbs to this prepiration as a lot of Algiarine pirates would melt before the onset of a British Naval squadron.

On Monday April 22nd the Gospel was preached here by Mr. R. E. Morley of Birkenhead, on the words "Be- lieve, Look, Take," whioh very clearly illustrate God's Gospel. The first word was used to the Fhilippian Jailor when he cried anxiously "What must Idoto be saved." We do not believe all we hear,we first ask who gives the report. God is the author of th's message which is worthy of acceptance. Belief of the message re- veals to our eyes our state as sinners bAore God and then Jesus se the sinners Saviour. To believe not mikes God a liar and causes Him to say the unbeliever is condemned already. The word "Look" gives four thought, it first exhorts us to lo At, it addresses us personally,it points to an object, Christ ; the result is silvation. "Take the water of life frec-ly" also gives three thoughts. Tne extent of salvation is for whosoever will ; its character is the wat-r of life for it gives life and sustains life. Flow is it given? Freely. If the salvation of God is so simple what must be the doom of those who reject it.

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Opening of a New Rostrum.
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyan Church. Opening of a New Rostrum.

A new rostrum was epened in Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday. The trustees had long bsen of opinion that certain alterations could with advantage be made to the existine pulpit, and that it might be ex- tended so as to give seating accommodation for ten or twelve persons, and thus avoid the erectien of the unsightly platform which it was found rep:liege to put up for public meetings, The original pulpit, which was of classic design, was designed in two heiehts an upper and lower deck ; the lower one projecting beyonn the upper, and being mostly used for week evening services, when the gallery of the church was not occupied. The existing scheme has been designed to bring forward the upper pertion into line with and over the lower portion, thus bringing the upper pulpit some three additional feet into the body of I the church. The whole of the beautifully marked mahogany frontage with its moulded panelline, shaped and carved trusree, has been retaiurd and made to pro- ject in the form of a bay some fifteen inches berond two aide wings, which have been elaberatety treeted with handsomely turned and carved open baluetrading carried on panelled and moulded framing and surmounted with a heavily moulded and ramped frieze and handrall,which will form a book board. The classic design of the pulpit, somewbat severe in' style, required that the extension should be carried out in strict accordance with the original scheme, and this has been done with marked' effeet,adding character and massiveness to the structure which the bpaciousuess of the church will fully permit. To counteract the effect produced by bringing forward the Rostrum nearer the congregation the height of tita floor has been reduced some fifteen inches. The whole of the new work has been executed in mahogany stained and polished te match the mistime portions of the pul- pit, which. have been retained, and the whole brought down to one uniform tint. The rostrum, which is semi- circular in plan, will give ample mccom:nodatien for all pureoses, and, besides adding beauty to the interior of the church, will meet a long-needed want. The work has been carried out in an able and efEzient inaener by Messer. G. and J.Weaver, cabinet makere, Bridge-street.
