APRIL 27TH 1960.

THE Queen's visit to Ireland The Queen's Visiteame to an end on Thursday, to Ireland. when she began her home- ward journey. It has been a remarkable visit in many ways. The idea was the Queen's own, and she has carried it out with an energy, an alertness, and a thoroughness most astonishing in a lady of her years. We have to remember, when we con- sider the visit as a whole, that her Majesty is of a ripe old age, burdened with the cares of State, and seeking change as one of the essential conditions of her physical health. Her visit has been conducted throng bout on the most enterprising lines, how- ever, and with as little conventionality as possible. Of course, there have been official events, and Dublin Castle has been as brilliant as in its best days. The Lord-Lieutenant has been managing affairs, and the notables have been thronging to Dublin and its vicinity, in order to show their pro- found respect for the good Sovereign who rules over them. But the QUEEN'S visit has been to the Irish people, and to every class of it, from the school children upwards. She has made no dis- tinction in this respect, and she has never for- gotten that Ireland is a Catholic country, and that most of her Catholic subjects have not a word te say against her character, her reign, or the influence she has exercised through society. It has been a pleasure to see her recognising the Catholic ecclesiastical dignitaries, and paying attention to the admirable Sisters who manage schools and instruct in various industries. This recognition has been marked by grace and naturalness, without any idea of condescension or humiliating patronage. In her drives and recep- tions the QUEEN has remembered that the Irish people have been attached to her personally, and that her Irish soldiers have fought successfully and with undaunted valour in support of the Empire and against her enemies. The primary object of her visit was to show the Irish people that she appreciated their devotion, and the im- pression she has made upon them has been uniformly good, and we believe it will be per- manent. "Poor neglected Ireland" is the note of many a pathetic ballad. It is not the fault of the Royal Family, however, that Ireland has fewer visits and fewer occasions of rejoicing in the fa yours that Royalty can bestow. We may accept it as established that the visit now ending has demonstrated that the Irish people have always stood high in the personal re- gard of the QUEEN, and that they now stand higher than they ever did before. They have given to her Majesty a hearty welcome, they have behaved themselves with the utmost propriety and they have proved that deep in their hearts there is a warm love for simple kindliness and for the person of their Sovereign. More was not demanded of them. The visit has not been political, and we have no desire to draw any political inferences from it. It has been a spon- taneous act of affection and admiration from the good Lady who reigns over Ireland, as she reigns over Great and Greater Britain, and the millions of India. It has been appreciated in this light by every Irishman who has been content to regard the visit properly. It has been a striking and an unqualified success, and we welcome home the I QUEEN with a deep loyalty and thankfulness for what she has been able to do.

IN the general disposi- Are British Officers t. on to blame our officers Stupid ?. for not avoiding am- bushes and averting disasters it is often thought sufficient. to say that they are stupid. An epithet flung out in this heated fashion seems to meet the necessities of the case, and it relieves critics and common people. But is it correct to use the word? Stupidity implies density, want of observation, in- ability to do the right thing at the right time. British officers are not dense. They are as intel- lectual as the officers of any other army in Europe. They are better able to understand many things because of their sporting habits and their open- air life. They are observant, and they do not need either pluck or dash. They know how to fight, as far as acting with their men is concerned, and they know how to die. But they are not trained in the art of observing an enemy and in the combinations of tact and method necessary to make good commanders against a wily and re- sourceful,foe. We kmve got to teach them these things by practising military operations on a larger scale, and selecting officers for experimental work. It would be well if we made an officer's life more laborious and businesslike. It ought to be a careerand not an opisode,the devotion of a life and not the diversion of a man of birth. It is prob- ably wrong of us to criticise our officers, as if they alone were to blame and we were innocent. Very many of the faults of our present military system are our own. We have b eon content to sleep on, and see the life, of an officer become a kind of fashionable way of go tting an occupation until Parliament could be entered or a title inherited. Our arrangements are made en the assumption that the upper classes ought to lead the army, and the other classes follow the upper classes. It is a false notion, but it was not begot in the brain of a stupid officer. it is one of the features of our constitution, and the i ndividual soldier who may be upbraided by the politician has always this crushing rejoinder at his command: "You Par- liamentarians make the army. We stupid officers don't." And, really, that settles the matter—for the present. Officers are made by the system, and the system has got to be altered. The British officer

with his individual daring, his resolution, his hero- 11 isrn,only needs to be better trained in handling men, in meeting new situations,and in the art and science of war, and he would simply be perfect. He is not stupid--he is only deficient in the finished train- ing of the businesslike soldier. Give him the train- ing, make it compulsory, encourage all talent, think less of society, use its influences less, thrust aside its pressure more valiantly, and the result would be satisfactory. Another point we must re- member—the use of smokeless powder. Our officers have bad to encounter troops using it for the first time. No other army in Europe has had the ex- perience. Its use makes observation difficult. We are meeting a force all cavalry. No European army has ever done this before in modern times. The country favours defence. Let us bear all these points in mind, and we shall use the word stupid less frequently, and absolutely decline to fasten it as a just epithet to all the men who hold commission; in the British Empire.

Lord Newton " talked straight" at the annual meeting of hiS constituents on Saturday, perhaps even straighter than suited the tastes of the audi- ence. The speech was made in support of a resolu- tion expressing unabated confidence in the G-overment, and the speaker want on to say that the country was not in the least indebted to that Government for the narrow escape it had had of being turned out of South Africa. "We owe our successes," ho said, "almost solely to the stubborn tenacity and the dogged courage of the British soldiers ; statesmanship and generalship have very

little to do with the -successes which- have bee-n achieved." His Lordship's sentirnents are ours. It is really refreshing to meet with a Conserva- tive member who is willing to admit that what credit there is due front the progress of the war, is not due to the Government. We should he in- clined to give a little of it to our generals,Roberts Buller, and White, but undoubtedly the bulk of it goes to the rank and file of all regi- ments, English, Scotch, Irish, Welsh, and Colonial whose courage and determination have been, beyond praise. To them we owe the fact that Britain still reigns supreme in South Africa, and to mal-adininistration, coupled with the machina- tions of Messrs. Rhodes, Jerneson and "the rest of the crew," as Lord Newton describes them, do we owe the war which is costing thousands of lives and millions of money. Lord Newton does not regard the war with any enthusiasm, and if he were pressed he might perhaps be got to admit that there would have been no war had the men at the head of affairs displayed statesmanship worthy ot the name. Though he spoke for the resolution he is evidently not a thick and thin supporter of the Govern ment,and his candour will no do him any harm with the more level-headed and sensible Tories in tly_! division. Unfortunately there is good reason to fear that those entitled to rank in this category 2re very much in the minority.

Since our last issue Warrington has been de- prived by death of one of her best-known and most honoured sons in the person of Alderman John Ed ward Wright, ex-Mayer of the Borough, who passed away at Southport on Wednesday. Deep and sincere regret at the news was everywhere manifested, for the late alderman was possessed of perhaps as many friends and as few enemies in his native town as any man cJuld well be. In public work he has rendered yeoman service as the memoir we publish elsewhere abundantly shows. Few men were better known, or better liked by all his acquaintances than "John Edward Wright," as he was familiarly called. His generous disposition, natural and ever-present courtesy,made him widely popular, and we are sure that the loss of & matt who so recently held the highest position in the town will be keenly telt by the whole of the inhabitants whether per- sonally acquainted with him or not. The most striking characteristic of the deceased gentle- man was, we venture tv think, his intense patriot- ism and love of his native town. Mr. Wright never

lost an opportunity of expressing his pride in being a Warringtonian, "born and bred," and his feeling for the" good old town" almost approached vener- ation. 1--i7,3 never forgot what he owed to the town of his birth, and his years of public service were characterised by an earnestness and deter- mination to advance its interests by every means
iu his power. For some time die state of his health has caused him to relax those exertions,but

it was not generally anticipated that death was near, and the sad 'lows came in the nature of a shock to the majority of townspeople—especially as he was here so recently as Thursday in last week. At this moment warm sympathy will be extended to his widow, whose period of married life has been so suddenly and sadly brought to an end. We join heartily in the general condolence with Mrs. Wright and the family of the late Alderman.

Mr. Pinero's defence of the modern play follows I on the time-honoured axiom of Macaulay. The author of" The Gay L -)rd Quex " is somewhat annoyed at the criticisms of Lord Halsbury Enid Sir Edward Clarke, particularly that of the Lord Chaa,cellor. And he answers in a very pretty vein. He accuses the outsiders of presumption in pass- ing judgment. "What," he says, with raised hands, "would the Lord Chancellor think were I to criticise his judicial appointment ? " But that by the way, and it is delicate satire. The real excuse for the passages in Mr. Pinero's plays which' are called in question is that they are true to nature. Lord Macaulay held that the indication of vice on the stage was not objectionable,provided that virtue was not held up to ridicule. It cannot be said that Mr. Pinero's comedies are vicious in that sense. They are modern portraits, with the ehiaroscuro of fashionable existence to-day. They do not moralise, but even the gay Lord Quex had his lessons as to the folly of dissipation. That many of the modern productions are, however essentially flippant and unsubstantial cannot be denied. They may do for an evening's change; but who could discuss the musical comedies of to-day as they discuss dramas in Germany ?

The Duke of Argyll's public career ceased with his illness at a meeting he was addressing in Glas- gow five years ago, and though he has occasionally been seen in the House of Lords since, it has only been as a figure—so noticeable because of the whiteness of his locks, the pallor of his face and the primness of his clothes. Probably if he had not dissented so much and so often he would have carriedjmuch more weight in politics than he did in later years, but a letter of protest from him against this or that new movement came to be re- garded as a corollary of the movement. His first mistake was in objecting so vehemently to Mr. Gladstone's Irish land proposals of 1881. How much more effective his denunciation of the Home Rule proposals would have been had his separation from the Liberal party dated, as did that of the Duke of Devonshire, Lord James of Hereford and Mr. Chamberlain, from the year 1885. In scien- tific books he was too diffuse, the same desire to discover as many fallacies as possible weakening his force. He was a man of conspicuous ability, but in an age of specialisation he was diffuse. The error marred his speech, of which the half was bet- ter than the whole, though there could be no doubt as to his talent as an orator. Not content with politics :and science, he even turned his attention to poetry , but there again lie part missed achieve- ment.

The Walker fountain which has been presented to Warrington has not taken quite as long to build as Rome did, but still it has taken an unconscionably long time to complete the struc- ture. Last year we were faithfully promised that we should see the gentle sprays of water flowing from innumerable jets by Walking Day. There must, however, have been a serious miscalculation for that annual festival has not only passed long since, but the children are already looking forward with pleasurable anticipation to the next. It is quite within tho range of proba- bility that the fountain will be completed some time this year for we are credibly informed

that orders have been given for the painting of it. That marks another stage in the progress of the work—and, we should think oLe of the last stages. ' Constructional operations are practically corn- pleted, as the long expected dolphins ai,d statues have at last arrived and taken up their allotted positions. A sigh of relief will go up when the unsightly scaffolding which has so long enease.d the fountain is taken away and it can be seen in all the glory of a new coat of paint. We hoso only one suggestion to affer, and it is as follows: Tile bands have started playing in the Park ;W not have the fountain playing at the same time

Warrington last week made a record of unenviable description. Within two days, gr' Brighouse, the county coroner, was called upr to preside at no fewer than eight inquests 1° the Warrington district. This is the largest 1111131- ber of inquests we have yet heard of in Warring: ton within so short a space of time. The nature °I the cases has also been of a startling, if not of. 5d shocking kind. Three men whilst of unsound null" have put an end to their lives by their own how', and each of them chose a different method .61' carrying out his purpose. One of them WI" gered a few hours in extreme agony aft°r taking a dose of carbolic acid; another shot a bullet through his right temPl° whilst the third hanged himself by a rel 39 which he used in his work as a porter. The three of the other inquests were on the bodies. el men who had died from injuries received whas° following their several employments and forcib.lY remind us that even peaceful industry claims .It'S victims. Even more pitiful were the remaining two cases for in both the names of the deceased persons were unknown. One of them died il.l barn and the other in a field, and they were burial without a relative in the world to follow them t° their last resting place. They were types of the; class which tramp the country from end to eau' and who never enjoy the blessings of home life' Let us hope, that in their last resting place, thei may be happier.

ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH. A most successful tea and social were held, on Wednesday evening, at the Shaw-street Schoolroom for the purpose ot augmenting the organ fund ot the St. Michael's Church. At the conclusion of an excellent tea and concort, games and dancing were indulged in until nearly midnight. •

WIDNES WHEELERS' CYCLE CLUB. About 25 members of this club had a very pleas- ant run on Thurpday last. They journeyed to Woolton, and stayed at the elephant Llotel, where a substantial tea was provided. Sulx.equently the wheelers indulged in bowls and billiards. They afterwards returned home, arriving safely after an enjoyable spin. GENERAL DISTRICT RATE FOR RUNCORN.

At—ii-We—cial meeting of. the Ittincorn Urban Dis- trict Council presided over by Mr. W Handley, J.P., on Tuesday night, the Seal of the Council was fixed to the general district rate for the year ending March 31st, 1901.—Mr Imison in moving the resolu- tion referred t 3 the satisfactory growth of the rate during the last year and said they had every reason to believe that that growth would be maintained. RIINPJORN BOITMEN IN TROUBLE AT ALTRINCHAM.

Before Mr R H Joynson and other marristrates, at the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Ivans, 24, Taylor's-row, lialton, Runcorn, a boat- man, was summoned for working a horse whilst in an unfit state at Broadheath, on April 7. Inspector Robinson, of the R.S.P.O A., and Constab!e Proctor deposed that the animal in question, a cream- coloured horse was attached to a canal flat. The horse was sutering from a couple of old sores, and the animal's collar, through pressing upon them, waS saturated with matter. The animal was quite unit for work and Inspector Robinson said it should have been killed. Defendant said the horse had in- jured itself through falling, but he had done his best for it, and he did not think he had been guilty of cruelty. He had since sold the horse. The Chairman said the Bench considered the case proved, and defendant would be fined 203 including costs. •

RBIs/CORN BOATING CLUB: The Easter holidays usually bring a rush of Run- corn Boating Clabites to the wall appointed Boat House at Rocksavage, but this year owing to the rough weather prevalent round and about April 16th only a few members more venturesome than the majority braved the elements; therefore it was Saturday afternoon last before the boating season could be considered open. The weather was ideal for rowing, although the banks of the Weaver have not yet arrayed themselves in their mummer beauty. At 5.30 13.132. the only things in the brat house were the trolley on which the boats are transferred to water and vice versa, and one or two sails. Every boat was in use and all well filled. There ware at least 50 members with friends up the stream on Saturday afternoon, arid in the evening when the boats returned, some behind erunner packets some behind Salt Union Packets, some behind two mules and two narrow boats, some still rowing manfully, old members felt serenely content, while new mem- bers were enthusiastic, with the afternoon's enjoy- ment.

MARRIAGE AT GARSTON.—BOSTOCK —HANDLEY. On Wednesday afternoon, at the Congregational Church, Garston, the marriage of Mr. Henry Join Bostock, the Oaklands, Stafford; with Miss Nora Handley, younger daughter of Mr. James Handley, J.P., C.C., Garston, was celebrated. The church, which had been tastefully decorated, was filled to overflowing, the bride's father being highly respec- ted in Garston and district, and there were also numerous friends from Staff Ird and Runcorn. The ceremony was performed by the Rev Thomas Cole (pastor), assisted by the Rev S B Handley, of Hert- ford, uncle of the bride. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a dress of ivory duchesze satin, trimmed with Brussels lace and chiffon, with full court train, and a tulle veil over a wreath of orange blossom. She carried a bouquet of choice exotica and lilies of the valley. The bridesmaids were Miss Handley (sister of Vie bride), Miss Ger- trude Bostock (si,ter of the bridegroom), and Misses Jessie Handley and Dolly Cameron (cousins of the bride,) Later the newly-married couple proceeded to London, en route for the Italian lakes. A. RITNCORN FOOTBALLER KICKED BY A. HORS E. William Gayter, a carter in the .employ of the Runcorn Co-eperative-ziociety, and a member of the "A " team of the Runcorn Football Club, was pro- ceeding up Bridge-street on Monday afternoon last in charge of a lurry laden with coal, to which two horses were attached. Gayter was leading the hems@ in the shafts, and when the tarry got opposite Hope Hall the chain horse suddenly became restive and lashing out with its hind legs, kicked Gayter ia the face knocking him senseless to the ground. Mr Garrett, the market inspector; and Mr Grice,saddler were quickly on the spot, and he injured man was picked up and carried into the market hall. Mr. Garrett rendered first aid, and in the meantime pro- fessional assistance was sought. Dr. Robinson eventually arrived on the scene, and ordered the man's removal to his home. The police ambulance was requisitioned for thig purpose,and,P.C.'s Bowyer and Wilson took the man to his residence. Gayter remained unconscious for some considerable time. On examination it was found that his left jaw was badly hurt, and several teeth were knockad out.

At the convivial function which was held at the conclusion of the Bradford (champions of the York- shire Northern Union League Competition) v. Rest of the League match, played on Saturday, presenta- tions were made of the cup and medals won by the first team and the shield and medals won by the second team.—The Chairman handed the Junior Competition shield, together wit:3 the medals, to Mr. J. H. Crompton (an old member of the Runcorn team), the captain of the Bradford A team, in recognition of the winning of this competition championship abo.—Mr. Crompton, in reply, said that second teams ought to be the natural recruit- ing ground of the first teams, and lie thought the Bradford Club had set an excellent example in this respect.—The remarks of Mr. Crompton cannot be too heartily endorsed. Tanks chiefly to the example and coaching influence of the old Run- cornian,the doable event•has been accomplished by the Bradford Club. so that the club now possesses two shields and sets of medals to testify to thAir all round prowess on the field of play. The (repres- sions nught t 3 be a self-evident proposition, but unfortunately many clubs have not the patience or the judgment to do so. If greater attention were paid to the development of young blood in the second teams of our leading clubs, the craze for importing talent would diminish in a natural way. div.p: CONTRACr TICKETS.

At the special meeting of the Runcorn Urban District Cpuncil held on Tuesday night, and at which Mr W Handley presided over a full attend- ance of members, Mr. P. A. Lake (law clerk) sub- mitted the following clause for the promoters of the Transporter Bridge which related to contract tickets :—" (1) The company may grant to passen- gers for the use of the bridge by this Act pasi tickets or family tickets at such rates on such terms and for such periods not exceeding one year as may be agreed upon or may issws books contain- ing any number of tickets at a reduced rate but so that no preference be given any person. Provided always that the company shall if required issue pass tickets entitling any foot passenger to use the bridge at all times when the same shall be open for traffic for a period not exceeding one weak, alai at a rate not exceeding one shilling, bat subject to such regulations as shall be prescribed by the com- pany . (2). A pass ticket shall not be transferable, and shall not be used by any person except the per- son to whom it is granted, atri a family ticketshall not be used by any person not being one of the family in respect of which it is granted, and any such pass ticket or tamily ticket shall not be used by any person after the period limited for its use. (3) If any person acts in any way in contravention of the provisions of this section or uses or attempts to ire any falser counterfeit ticket he shall for each offence be liable to a penalty not exceeding twenty shillings."—On the motion of the Chairman seconded by Mr Wilson, the clause was agreed to as accept- able to the Council. !.SK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATIIRS.—Advt.

div.head: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.
Three Days Sale of Work at Runcorn. LADY BROOKE PERFORMS THE OPENING CEREMONY.

On Wednesday, Thursday and Friday (to-day) a most successful sale of work has been in progress at the Mersey Mission Sono°lroom, Station-road, Run- corn. Its object is to raise funds for the pur- pose of cleaning, painting, and ventilating the sea- men's Institute. _ _ _ _

The history of the cause is brimful of interest, so that it will not be out of place to quote here the in- teresting facts got together and published in the programme of the bazaar :—" Previous to the open- ing of the Mission Room at Bottom Locks in the year 1875, there was a small Mission Church called St. Peter's, supported by the late Countess of Ellesmere, served by a Curate with surpliced choir, etc., under the charge of ,the late Vicar, Canon Barclay. When the Bridgewater Trustees trans- ferred the Canal property to the B. N. Co. Ltd., St. Peter's was cloie I for a considerable time, and re- patteined so until 1875,when the late Thomas Beddows rlsq, the resident agent of the B. N. Co, together with Rev Canon Barclay and Dr, Preston. thought that it was necessary that a Nlission RO3in be opened for the use of the tinting population, which was increasing rapidly. Accordingly com- munications were opened with the Mersey Mission to Seamen at Liverpool, and an application made to the Committee of teat Society to send a Missionary to Runcorn. In the event of this being done the above-named three gentlemen promised to place St. Peter's Church at their disposal for the use of a Mission. The Mersey Mission C3l:l2olitteie acceded to this request and appointed Mr W Shaw as their Missionary, and in 1875 Mr Shaw commenced his labours at the port. In course of time the trade of the port increased so much, and the work of the Mission progressed so rapidly that the need of larger premises became apparent. The old room was in- capable of enlargement and the extension of the docks rendered it unsuitable. Fortunately a very suitable freehold site in Station-road, Itancorn near the locks was acquired and the present handsome building was erected on it: The ceremony of lay- ing the foundation stone of the new institute was performed by the Right Hon. Lord Egerton, of Patton, on April 16th, 1891, aad was opened on the 10th December of the same year, by the Right Rev the Lord Bishop of Chester. The work of the mis- sion progressed most satisfactorily, and to an ex- tent far beyond anticipation. The institute, the doors of which are thrown wide open to the sailors of every nationality and of every creed, and ako to the canalboat people who visit the port,has proved a great boon. The reading room is much more fre- quented. The weekly concerts and entertainments during the winter months have been well attended, and have become a refuge and eounter attraction to the temptation which surround seamen during their time ashore.'

As stated, with the object of further enabling the con- tinuance of such good work, under acceptable conditions, the large schoolroom had been handsomely laid out with attractive stalls, replete with the handiwork of the good workers connected with the Institute; other stalls were weighed down with sweetmeats and flowers; then again there was the ever present refreshment stall. In close proximity to this was some device of skill ; upon the stage was a ginsy tent wherein the venturesome could be brought face to face with the mystic unknown. The whole was a well arranged bazaar, and did great credit to the ladies present, who waited anxiously the com- mencing of tne sale and the advent of customers. The First Day. The chair was taken on Wednesday afternoon, by Mr. Charles Bushell (chairman of the Mersey Mission to Sea- men),Liverpool,and in the preeence of a large attendance of sympathisers and work ars at the mission, he said it gave him great pleasure, as chairman of the Mersee ' Mission to Seamen, of which the Ssanzan's Institute, Runcorn, was a branch, to be present. He would not say he was there to introduce Lady Brooke to them, bscause it was more than likely her ladyship was better known to them than himself. He was there t ask Lady Brooke to open the bazaar and also to thank her for doing so, and also to tell her how thankful and how much obliged they were to her for giving them her kind help. 'nay were all well aware that the Mersey Mission to Seamen was a branch of the Great Lendoa Mission to Seamen, and it was a very important branch, having branches itself at Garston, Ellesmere Port, Birkenhead, and,net the last,nor theleast worthy and active Breech, was the ens at Runcorn. Runcorn he was proud to say, was indeed almost self supportifig, for they barna that if Runcorn were in need of arything or there was anything to be done, Ruecorn always appeared to be independent of Liverpool. Indeed,when that building was erected, with the exception of a very small grant fora site it was almost wholly erected at the expense of Runcorn itself. (Applause.) That Was not all; for the people of Runcorn, appreciating the work of Mr. W. Shaw, set to building him a house (which they gave into the charge of trustees) and put him into it, where he then lived very comfortably, thanks to his Runcorn friends. (Applause.) He thanked the Runcere people heartily for having done so much. The Mission had a great number of kind friends,not the least of whom was Mr. Dives, their hon. secretary. (Appleusp.) In concluding, Mr Bushell referred to the fact that tee were a great mercantile nation and greatly dependent upon our seamen. It should be a pleasant duty, there- fore, to all to do what they could for the men who heed so many and manifold dangers whilst at sea and so many temptations whoa on shore. They could give them a home, a shelter, and recreation when they came from their voyages. Having also referred to the noble manner in which the mercantile servics had carried about 150,000 of our soldiers a distance of 7,000 miles, and to the excellent services of the Naval Brigade which so ably assisted in the fighting against the Boers, Mr. Bushell pointed out there were addi-ennel reasons why all should do their best for the sailor. (Appleuse.) He had pleasure in calling upell Lady Brooke to open the sale. Lady Brooke, who was received with quite an ovation first of all expressed the great pleasure she had in coming to Runcorn, for people were always very kind ; but, it was especially a pleasure to Come to a place where they all knew a most excellent work was being carried on. (Applause.) All those good works, however, required money and ' though there were many strains upon everyone's heart strings and purs. strings hr the help of the widows and orphans and relatives of the poor soldiers and sailors fighting in S auth Africa, she hoped they would be sue- cessfial in their venture. Referring to her own eon- section with the War Fend her ladyship said she ceuld bear testimony to the noble example of generosity that the people of Runeorn had showa—especielly those wino sot aside a email portion of- their weekly earnings for the cause. She was most heartily gratified by the large and hearty response of the people of Runcorn. (Applause.) All these good causes took money and it generally followed that those who supported one good Cause liblad also to supeort others. She trusted that people would come forward that afternoon and support those who had woxle?d so hard to get up the sale of work, and if they did she was sure there would be sufficient funds te get the institute renovated and repeiredas it so much needed. • RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A. COR,RESPONDENT]. The improvement of the higiaviray at and about ASGCCO3r Bridge has now come to a dead-lock, owing to the fact that the figure asked by Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., for land necessary to carry out the improvement is too high. I learn that the sum asked is £l5OO, with a return of £250 upon certain conditions, which, by the way, are said to be unac- ceptatile.

One is, however, gratified to find the County Oouncil have been good onongh to exhaustively in- quire into the method of remedying the highway in this importint place. They have come to the decision that the present bridge is inadequate, and opened neptiations with a view to the erection of a better and more commodious bridge. This the public can see the County Council now practically admit re ipon3ibility for all they have complain° i about; and we may also be assured it will only be a matter of time before some remedy is forthcom- ing. As the new lodge will cost over £2,000, in addition to the £1,500 already mentioned for the land, the County Council should be commended highly on all sides for their circumspection, In the meantime the landlord may see his way to come down in price, for not only will the public be bene- fited, but his own property will be considerably en- hanced in value by the projected bridge.

Runcorn publicans are brought face to face with a very humane request this week, and that it "to re- frain from serving one man with liquor." Is it too much to ask? The individual whose drink supply they are requested to cut off is one well known to them, and one whom I feel sure th4y would not for one moment wish to suffer through any action of theirs. They are called upon,as it were,to make one compulsory teetotaler,and should they succeed they will be doing a good service both to themselves, to the individual, and to the town.

The Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Bill will soon be fairly on its way through the second chamber. A new clause was accepted by the Runcorn. Urban District Council on Tuesday evening last, which provides foi7 contract tickets, pass tickets,and family tickets. The terms of the clause appear in another cliumn,and a glance at it will at once show that the District Council have "gotten more than they asked" in respect to cheap tickets, etc. Nothing, however, but a practical test will prove the benefits offered but, prima facie, they appear decidedly generous.

The dangers of rambling in and about Stonehills —a rocky place abounding in worked out quarries near Runcorn—have been illustrated this last fort- night by a most peculiar accident the ptirticulars of which I era unable to exactly arrive at. What is common knowledge, however,is that a certain well- known young gentleman accompanied by a lady went strolling in that direction with the result that the lady fell down a" slump " a matter of about 20 to 30 feet, and severely injured her leg. There are some not very pleasant stories about, concerning, the gagging of the Press in the matter, and I there- fore give the above to somewhat exonerate myself.

The chairmanship and vice-chairmanship of the Runcorn Rural District Council have not changed hands, and neither have the like honours of the Board of Guardians undergone any change. The first two honours are possessed by Messrs J Knowles, J.P., and Samuel Woodward, and the lat- ter by Messrs J Moseley-Williams and J Stokes. Toe re-appointment was most unanimous,a matter upon which all four gentlemen deserve hearty congratu- lations. Personally. I sfoll hold toll it these honour.; should go the rounds, and low/ for the time when the District Council. and Board of Guardians will drop their conservatism in this matter.

speaking of the Transporter Bridge, in giving Ws report upon the Parliament Committee's delibera- tions. Mr J Mclntyre sounded a rather selfish note, when he spoke of the only interest " they "—.-the District Council—"had in the matter was the inter- eats of the agriculturalists on the Cheshire side," and as a matter of fact all discourse tended in the same direction. It is a great pity that the Council agreed with him, for really one would think "their interests', should embrace all those of the general public, and not the agricultural section only Furthermore, the Cheshire farmer should be alive to the fact that the Lancashire farmer will use the bridge too, to compete against him on his o tvn ground. The understanding asked for with the pro- moters of the bridge is, however, wood one and both sides might eventually benefit by it.

Mr. W Handley at the conclusion of the Library Committee meeting, the other night, said he had seen Mr Woods, the engineer, and Mr Webster (of the Transporter Bridge seheme),and they had prom- ised that when the model of the bridge was done with by the House of Lords Committee, they would be pleased to forward it for exhibition to Runcorn. Mr Woods also would be pleased to lecture on the bridge and indeed upon bridges in general. I hope this opportunity will present itseli soon, for a de- monstration of this interesting topic would be most opportune Let us hope if it is to be. the Library Committee will undertake to make the date well- known, and carry out the proceedings upon similar lines to their recent excellent lectures.

The Gilchrist Lectures for which Runcorn had made application will not fall to our lot this year, nor perhaps next but a very favourable letter has been received from the trust intimating that Run- corn's application would be favourably considered another year. The delay is, of course,to be regretted but we can console ourselves that we are still better off than many other towns.

John Leach, licensee of the Fox Tavern, Alcock- street, Runcorn,was summoned at the instance of the police for permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises on the 26th of March last.—Mr. Fletcher (solicitor) Northwich, prosecuted, and Mr. A. Browne (solicitor) Warrington, defended. In opening the case Mr. Fletcher said the charge was one ;with which the Runcorn Bench of Magis- trates were familiar. The Fox Tavern was a beer house situate in Alcock-street,Runcorn, and he was informed that its license was granted previous to 1.869. The penalty for an offence of the description they were arguing before the court was £lO (not exceeding) for the first offence, and for a second conviction the penalty could be increased to £2O. This, however, was the first offence alleged against the defendant and he thought when their worships had heard the evidence they would be satisfied the offence had been committed. Briefly the facts were, on Monday the 26th of March two men named •Basnett and Whittle—(he noticed in his friend's list of witnesses those names, so no doubt the men would be called)—who were bricklayers, and who had work to go to on the day in question, and who had had their railway fare furnished to them by their employer so that they could have pro- ceeded to Frodsham where their services were required, called at the house. lie would sub- mit evidence enough from which the Bench (mild deduce that these men had been drinking at the house almost all thea...elar. They were seen to enter the house between 7 ant 8 o'clock in the morning. The police found them there between 3 and 4 o'clock in the afternoon at which time both Basnett and Whittle were drunk. The police warned the landlord and the land- lady and told them even then the condition of the men was such that they would have to furnish a repert. Their wecships would have thought that weuli have been sufficient. But on entering the house again at 5-35 p.m. the officers found the two men were again there in a drunken condition. On the second oecaeion they Lad pint cups of liquor in taeir hanos. Tne men were requested to leave and after some demurrence on their part they were got out of the house and into Fryer-street. They there created such a disturbance, however, that the paLce had no other alternative only to bring them to the Police Statien. They were brought before the m leis- trate the following morning, and fined, but they decided to go to Knutsford for 14 days rather -than pay: The charge upon which they were convicted was one of drunkenness. Another feature of the case to which attention would be drawn was the condition of the land- lord—he would not say he was drunk—but he was in such a muddled cendition as not to be thoroughly cap- able of looking after his house properly. Sergeant William Ceoper,of the Runcorn Censtebulary swore from information received he visited the For Tavern on the 28:h of Marce at 315 in the afternoon'. He was accompanied by Acting•Sargeant Gregory and Constable Wylie. They entered the lobby of the home first and then proceeded to the bar. There were five men there including Basnett„ Whittle, and Huggine,three men whom he knew. There were four pint mugs on the table and another on the counter. His attention was directed to B isnot who was on his feet, rocking from side to side and trying to sing. He was decidedly drunk. He also saw the man, Whittle, sitting in a corner by the fire. He was also drunk to judge by his appear- ance. Mrs. Leach was in charge of the bar. He called her attention to the men and said " Mrs. Leach they are drunk." Mrs. Lsach made no reply. The man Whittle got off his chair and made an effort to stand aaylog he was not drunk, after which he eat down again. Witeess then asked for the landlord land subsequently he came. Mr. L meh said " What's up sergeant ?" He then told him about the two men Basnett and Whittle saying they were drunk and he ad- vised Leach to get them off the premises. Leach then ordeeed the men off. Previous to going off Whittle and the othar man finished drinking their beer. Whittle left the house first, staggering a bit; by the back door in the the direction of Cobley's lodging-heuse. He and Ser- eeaut Gregory followed him. They then returned to the public-house and found that Basnett had not gone, so he, again advised the landlord to get him off the premises.' Mr Leach told the man to go and thou passed the re- mark to witness " that he did not think they were s) bad and heped that he (the sergeant) would look over it that time." Witness replied that he would be obliged to report the ca.e, to which Mr Leach said he was very sorry it had occurred--Though subject to a very lengthy cross-examination by Mr Browne,the witness adhered to his original statement.

Acting-Sergeant Gregory corroborated the previous witness, adding that at 5.35 he visited the house again accompanied by P.C. Wylie. He entered the same room ac upon the first visit and found Charles Whittle and IS twat there again. they had beer again before them this time the pint cups being in their hinds. Whittle was leaning against the counter, and Basnett was sitting down. When he entered Whittle said " What did be want following them for. Did he want to lock them up ?" using foul language at the time. vVitnai,s then aceosting the landlord told him he ought to be ashamed of himself, having the men on his premis,s after what the sergeant had told him in the morning. Upon that the landlord went into the bar and ordered the men out saving" now Whittle you will only rt me in trouble; get on outside." The two men drank up their liquor and Whittle said he would not go out. Witness then said to the men "you will get the landlord in trouble as well as yourselves "Whittle went out first and Basne.tt followed him. On getting outside bo:Ilo the men began arguing the point and creating a disturbance in consequence of which they were obliged to look them up. They were brought before Mr. Wis. , wall the following morning.—Cross-exaMined by Mr. Browne: He heard nothing said about a time-table,but he did hear something 'said about the men wanting to 'go to pion K)p to work for someone else. The men were kept in the parade room alb= 25 minutes before they were locked in the cells so that the superintendent should see them. When the superintendent did eee them he did not mike Basnett walk a line to see whether he was drunk.
Police-Constable Wylie comborate I both prey:oos witnesses.

James Crank, labourer, Lockeitreet, Runcorn, said on the 26:h of March he was in the employ of Mr. Cobley, of Fryer-street. He was deptry and had the run of the kitchen. He began work about 7 o'clock in the morning and hat seen the man Whittle who lodged at Cobley's go to the Fax Tavernit would be a little before S o'clock. He knew Bisnett also, He went into the Fox to tell Whittl something or other, and whilst there had a glass of b 3er and Whittle had a pint. Barlett came in shortly after- wards. He left the Fox abut twelve o'clock. •He did not see any of the men again until he saw them about 3 o'clock. Whittle, who was then in the house, acted in a drunken manner. In his opinion both men were cer- tainly drunk. Whittle left the lodgings again about half-past four, and as he was leaving witness advised him not to go to tti. public-house again--By Mr Brown: He did not give information to the police and had no:, seen Greeory that day. There was ne jealousy between Coblet'e house and the Fox, mad he dented that was the cause of any infoimation being given the police. Superintendent Pearson, testified to seeing the men Whittle and 13/matt at the p vale room. Ile was qaite sure both were drunk when be saw them. As a matter of fact the men were seldom sober and were well-known in the town.—By Mr. Browne : Mrs. Leach had had an interview with him. Mrs Leach did not state the men were not drunk ti him, but she inferred it. Sne asked hint ii her husband was going to be summoned and he told her that it did not rest with him but with the Cnief Constable but the men were not going to be charged that neerning with being drank on licensed premises, and as a matter of fact they were not. Questioned by Mr. Browne respecting a report which was abroad that at first the Polize Officers' statements did not =agree. Superintendent Pearson said that the only particular in which they aid not agree was with respect to one of the men standing and the other hitting, but that point had subsequently been feasibly accounted for. , For the defence Mr. Browne argued in cases of that nature there mast naturally be a good deal of contra- i an. The defence would be that the men were per- fectly sober,but even assuming that the men were drunk he asked, if in the face of the ten or tw ell?'" witnesses the Bench would hear that day, and they would probably take two or three hours to decide whether the men were drunk or not, hew was a poor publican who had got to make lip his mind in an instant to decide so difficult a point. Further more was it likely that the lieensee would risk practically his living for the sake of the little to be desired by serving the men. He would produce evidence to prove that the men were.in the repidion of several in- dependent witnesses, perfectly sober, and that they hail been served with but two pin's to one, and one pint, t ) the ether, and that on the second coming to the house the men had only come for the purpose of ascertaining what time they could get a train to go t. their their work at Frodsham.

, Cectli% Leach, wife of the defendant, said she was at- tending to the bar of the Fox Tavern on the 26 h of March last. She saw Basnctt and Whittle come to the bouse in the morning. Whittle came to ask for Basnett, , and had a pint of beer. There were a number of other men re:so preseo 1. Basnett subsequently had a pint of beer. The two men were only in the house for a few minutes and then they went out. She saw them again about three to half-past three,but they had not remained in the house from eight until that time. The men walked into the house. and neither showed any signs of having had drink. Whittle did nat have any drink upon the second visit, as he said he had been very ill all the week end and was then very bad. She believed that Basnett had another pint of beer. She remembered Gre2ory and Cooper coming in when she was in the bar. The bar and parlour were in the same room being only divided by a counter. Whittle was sitting down, and Basnett Iwas alsa seated on a small chair. Neither of the rn:n had drink before them then. Gregory, at least she thought it was Gregory. said to her, "these men are drunk ?" She replied "They are

not drunk" Gregory then said "Where's your hus- band 2" Witness replied "In the cellar tapping beer." Subsequently she called her husband. The officers then told her husband that the two men were drunk, but he replied they were not. The two men went out whilst the police were there. She saw the men next (for the third time) about five o'clock. Basnett came and spoke to her and asked her what time there was a train to Frodsham, adding they had some work to do and were going to Frodslaarn over night ready to commence work 'in the morning. Whittle was with him. She was just going for the guide when the police came in, through the front door. Shortly before the police came in, a couple of painters who were working upstairs came down and said somsthing to them. No one else load been serving in the bar that cbsy but herself. She had not served the men with any drink and they had not asked for any so that if the police said they had pint cups in their hands they were saying what was untrue. Sergeant Gregory then told the men they would have to gl witlh himl ,‘ Well" he said "the men are not drunk and it is a shame." Referrir.g, to her interview with the Superintendent of Police she said that she was given to understand that tbe men were not going t) be proceeded against ctherwise she would have employed a lawyer. The Superintendent said to her "If I were you I would go home and take no further notice of this, perhaps you , will hear no further abut this."
Superintendent Pearson .aid he did not say so. Cross-examined by Mr. Fletcher, this witness adhered to her statement.

Joseph B tenet% bricklayer, said he had been twice convicted by the Court and fined 5s for drunkenness he thought. It was, about 9 o'clock when he called at the Fox in the morning. He had nothing to drink. He went to see if Whittle was there, and to tell him they could not go to Frodsharn, as the girders from Messrs. Timmin's had not been sent. Tney did not stay long at the Fox, and subsequently he went for a walk round the town. Whilst going round the town Whittle bought some meat and potatoes to make potato hash with, and upon tuning into lodgings after dinner, Whittle set atoat doing it. He peeled potatoes all right and put them to simmer by the fire. They then went again to the Fox and Whittle had a glass of beer. After being sent away by the police they went again to the Fox Tavern and were ultimately locked up —Mr Browne had hard work getting any- thing coherent out of this witness, and remarked he was sorry for any publican in Runcorn' who had that c'ass of witness to deal with.—CrosE-examined by Ur. Fletcher witness's narrative became hopelessly tangled and he inclined either to Mr. Fletcher or Mr. Browne at will.

Testimony as to the sobriety of the men Whittle and Basnett was Oven by Thomas Dawson, farm labourer, in the employ of Mr. Baguley, Manor Farm; Arthur Lea, Ann William Boden, painters in the employ of the Bed. ford Brewery, Company ; Joseph Field, carter • John M lyneux, drayman' in the employ of the Bedford Brewery Company; Thomas Hill, 47, Egerton-street milk man in the employ of the Chethire D tiries ; and Martha Ann Dillon, wife of Thomas Dillon, chimney sweep, a neighbour. The latter deposed to seeing the police officers escort the men to the police station. When they came out of the Fox Tavern there was no disturb- ance that she saw and the men went quiet enough. In her opinion they were perfectly sober. After a quarter of an hour's retirement the Chairman said they had given the case the best consideration they could, and were of opinion that a case had been made out. Leach would be fined 204 and costs £3 31 H. The license, however, wood not be endorsed. The Bench also expressed the hope that Mr. Leach would in future try and conduct his house more in cenformizy with the licensing laws.

div.head: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.
div.p: RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The first meeting of the newly-elected Committee was held on the Library premises on Tuesday evening. There were present :—Messrs W Handley, E Imison, D Bis- brown, W J Cunningham, E W Hutton, W Hankinsou, and J D Jones (librarian).

div.head: ELF= XI OF CHAIRMAN.
div.p: ELF= XI OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. W. Handley who was voted to the chair pro tem' proposed that Mr. S. Pope be the Chairman of the Committee f4r the ensuing year. He thought Mr. Pope would bo a crecl4; to the office. He hid filled the position of vice-chairman during the past twelve months, and he t'3ought he ought to be promoted. Mr. Cunningham seconded. He knew of no one who was better qualified to fill the office. The proposition was carried unanimously. THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Hopkinson moved that Mr Bight') wn be the vice- chairman. He had filled the office of chair.—ac prior to Mr Handley, and he served them well. It was on advantage to have a member of the Council in one of the official positions so that ho might pilot the minute's through, when they came before the Council. _ _
Mr:ltnison sedonded and referred to Mr Biibrown's usefulness when he occupied the position of chairman. The motion was carried unanimously. Mr. Bisbrown briefly acknowledged the compliment.

div.head: BOOKS PRESENTED.
div.p: BOOKS PRESENTED.

The librarian reported that the books presented during the month were:—By the trustees of the British Museum, " The Book of the Dead," being facsimiles of the Papyri of Hunefer, Anhai. Kerasher, and LetchemTt with sup- plementary text from the papyrus of Nu,with transcripts and translations etc.. by Prof. E A Wallis Budge ; from Stubbs' Publiching Company,Limited—Stubbs Directory 1900 ;Mr C B Hollinsworth, " Zion's Works," 3 vols. (iros. 4, 5 and 6); London and Paris Exchange Limited, Stock Exchang- Ropnrt ; Weekly Library Report from Hoye ; from W E Peck, " Peck'a Circular," Trades Direc- tory and Detailed Buyers' Guide to the Manufacturers of Birmingham and District. The Librarian observed that "The Book of the Dead" was a fine work. During the month of Minh the library was open 22 days, and the issues were as fellows :—Theology, 33; philosophy, 10 ; science, 56; history, &lAN) ; poetry, 10 ; fiction, 1,610 ; miscellaneous, 146 ; reference, 58 ; French literature, 1 ; music, 8 ; total, 2,032 ; showing a decrease of 71 on the corresponding,r. month of last war.
NEW BOORS FOR LIBRARY.

Mr. Handley,reftrrinv, to a list of bobs recommended for purchase by the Books Selection Clmmittee. said the amount proposed to be expended was £29 13s lid,£2s of that sum being for local books that they had been for- tunate enough to have offered to them at peels which he thought were a good investment. They were books that their library ought to possess and which they could not hope to get in the ordinary way at the price. He moved that the recommendation be adopted. Mr. Hankinson seconded and said he had seen some of the books. They ware of rare value, and would bu an acquisition to their library. The recommendation of the committee was adopted.

The books included among others wore the following: —Phillip's Views of Lancashire and Cheshire; Batenham and Musgrove's Ancient Chester (etchings) ; Coeshire Domesday Book ; Liverpool Bay (four volumes); Roman Lancashire (Watkin.); Liveroool Privateers; Eirwaker's E Ist Cheshire (2 volumes); Morris' Chester; LiverpooLby an old stager; Gamlin's Birkanhetd ; Liverpool Cele- britieS ; Bird's Eve View of Liverpool; Lord de Tabley's Flora of Oneshire ; Fonwicle. Chester; Lancashire and Cheshire Historic Society 0.7 volumes); Liverpool Liter- ary and Philosophical - Society (26 volumes) ; Bane's Liverpool, and Brereton's Cheshire Ordinance.
THE FINANCIAL STATEMENT. A YEAR'S EXPENDITURE.

The librarian submitted a statement of accounts for the year ended March 31st, 1900. The receipts were : Fines,-26 Si 71 ; tickets, £5 12s 23 ; papers and waste paper sold, £2 13s 21; members subscriptions. £1 is ; lost and damaged books, is 61; donations, £5 Os 6.1 ; from Free Library Rate, £l9l 73 ; balance, March 31st, 1899, lie 11d, total £212 12i 101. div.head: THANKS TO THE RETIRING CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THANKS TO THE RETIRING CHAIRMAN.
Mr. Cunningham in very eulogisae terms moved a hearty vote of thaulci to Mr W Handley, their last year's chlirman. •
Mr. Hankinson seconded.

Mr. JD Jones, the librarian, asked permission to add a tribute to Mr Handley's worth. No one had taken a greater interest in the library than had Mr W Handley, and he (the librarian) th,ught the year's acquisition of local hooks would 'alone show how interested Mr Handley had been in trying to make the Library more worthy of the public thau ever it had been before. (Applause,) Mr F W Hutton also snoported what had been said.

Mr Handley responded and expressed the extreme Dieasurn it had given him to be tho Chairman of the Library Committee a position he had now to resign on account of the greater honour conferred upon him. By that of course he did not mean to he-little the position of chairman te that committee. What he had been able to do had been a pleasureable duty. He thanked them all heartily for their vote of thanks and for the kind re- marks with which they perr+rded
BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLAM.

Mr. T. Simiter presided over a largely attended social gathering of the Brunswick Mutual Improve- ment Class, held on Wednesday evening, at the Brunswick schoolroom. In a brief address delivered during the course of the evening he referred to the source of instruction and amusement the meetings of the classes had been week after week and the beneficial influence they bore upon young minds. Mr J D Jones (vice-president) was also present.— After justice had been done to a capital tea, for which the young ladies of the class were respon- sible, a convivial evening was spent. Songs were contributed by Miss Bitty Carter who eang"Auntie," Mr. Thomas Johnson who gave "The sailor's sweet- heart," and Mr. George Pennington and others. Parlour games were played and other amusements indulged in so that when the company broke-up all had thoroughly enjoyed themselves. ASK or CUNNINGHAM' HIGH-CLASS MINERAL WATEES-44dvt.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
AN INCREASING NCISANCE-NIORC FOOTBALLING IN THE
STREET.

At the Wartingt3n Police Court on Monday, before Mr F Monks and other magistrates, Charles Baird, Queen-street, Robert Allen. 17, Kendrick-street, and Thomas Lawton, 4, Kendsick-street, youtbs! were sum- moned for playing lootball in Queen-street, to the annoyance of passeagers on the 13:h April.—P.C. Turner stated that at 11 a.m. on the date in question he was on duty in plain clothes in company with P.C. Clough awe saw the three defendants, in company with several others, playing at football on the fair ground. The ball came into the street and a young lady had a narrow escape of being struck in the face with it. He badcautioned the defendants twenty minutes previously. —The Chief Constable infcrmed the magistratss that there were no less than 15 psrsens summoned that morning for playing football in the streets. It was a growing nuisance and the penalties inflicted did not seem to have the slightest influence. He pressed for a substantial penalty.—Defendatrs were each fined 10s.—James Potts, 1, Turner's- yard, John Girt ledge, 27, Turner-street, andl Thomas Ireland, 34. Hind-street, were summoned for al similar offenee in 'Diener-street on the 13. h inst.—De-, fendants, who had not been previously cautioned were fined 7s 6i each.—James Simister, 71, Laira-street,l Ernest Dealey, 158, Longford -street, Thomas Ellis, 73.1 Watkinostreet, and John Burton, 88, Orford-lane, were summoned for a like offence in the rear of Laira-street and Forshaw-screet on the 15th inst.—P.C. Penniogtm proved the case and a fine of 7s 6J was imposed.— Robert Critchley, Yorke•treet, and Jam a Sherratt, York-street were fined 7s 6J and Thomas Sherratt,York- street, Thomas Gilbe.t Querinbv,3l, New-road and John Cliffe, 4,York-street were fined -54 for playing at football in York-street on the 17th April.—P.C. Clough proved the case'—At the close of the hearing of the cases. tee Chairman said the Bench were net going to inflict email penalties as they would not step the nuisance. They should go on increasing the floes till such conduct was put a stop to. The full penaity was 40s and costs. THEFT FROM BEWSET FORGE. At the Warrineton Police Court on Tuesday, before Alderman Sutton ene Mr. Birchall, Michael Mulligan was charged with st .eling from a cabin at Bewsey forge sometime between 5-30 and 10-30 on Monday night a bucket cont-ining a quantity of brass and lead of the value of £2, the property of the Pearioa and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limit at —He pleaded guilty.— The Chief Conrtable reeated the facts of the case from which it appeared that the prisoner had been employed off and on for a considerable tineo.at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles forge. He had not been working there however for some days past. He was last employed under a man named Kelly at the Beweey siding, in un- loading trucks which contained scrap itoe Sze. It was part of his duty to separate any lead and brass that might be found in the waggons and take it t 3 tbe store. On Monday the bucket containing brass and lead was seen by Kelly safe in the cabin on the Bewsey siding at 5-30. Later in the evening the cabin was locked up and the key was put on the top of the cabin as usual so that any workmen who had busi- ness there would know here it was and be able to open the door. The prisoner having worked there would know that and he appeared to have taken advantage of It to steal tbe brass and lead. At 10.30 he was met near Bewsey Forge be Sergeant Bell carrying a bucket on his shoulder. The sergeant noticing that the bucket was heavy challenged him and asked him where he had got it from. The prisoner immediatele threw it down and took to his heels. The sergeant followed and in Stam- ford-street blew his whistle. P.C. Monks was coming along the street and stopped the prisoner and toek him into custody. At the Police Station the prisoner made a clean breast of the theft. —Prisoner said he was drunk or he would not have, committed the offence.—The man Kelly spoke as to the prisoner's character and said he was always a bard working man.—Prisoner yens fined 103 and costs with the alternative of 14 days' imprison- ment.

WARRINGTON BOYS BREAK. INTO A ERNCOTE. At the Vs arrintttort Pmice Court on Wednesday before Alderman Sutton and other magistrates three boys nasned Albert Ernest Gough, 14, Baxter-street, John Ryder, 8, Baxter-street, aud James Bird, 18, Atherton-street, were charged with stealing from a bencote in the yard of Robert JoLer, 19, Baxter-street, at about 5 &clear on Monday afternoon twelve eggs valued at is., his pro- perty.—The Chipf Constable stated the facts of the case. On Monday alt.:7[loon at 4.30 Mrs. Joneg, the wife of the prosecutor. iPtt the house for the purpose of going into town. At that time the hencote in the yard was quite secure. There were two sittings of eggs under two haus which were prize bantams and the eggs were of consider- able value. Mrs. Jolies returned about forty minutes later and on going into the yard found that the hencote had been broken into. Two penes of glass in the window wore smashed and some of the woodwork had been damaged. The eggs were missing. Shortly afterwards the boy Gough came to her and brougaz her two eggs. He said it as not he who bad broken into the hencote but the boy Ryder. latorrna• ion was given to the police and the boys were apprehended by P C's Stuart and Carter. On being charged Gough said that he and Ryder broke into the cote. He (Gough) took an egg and threw it on the B.ooe. He hit ahe on the head with a stick to knock it off the nest. The boys appeared to have destroyed the eggs when they got them—rho prisoaer Ryder said there were only tint- e eggs.—lt was stated that Gaugh and Ryder had been before the court 80 recently as tha 9th of the present mouth when they were fined 21 6d for throwing stonrs.—Prisoners were ordered to receive 12 strokes of the birch rod.

MONDAY,—Before Messrs. F. Monks (h) th chair), S. Wright

T. Birchall. and J W. Hayward. A SOLDIER Stare TO GAOL.—John Hallman, a soldier, was charged with making use of obscene language in Batter- market-street at B.hS on. Saturday night. He was further charged with indecent behaviour and with aesaulting John Lester, a boy.—Alfred Down, a newsagent carrying on busi- ness in Church-st-eet. said that he was walking along Scot- land-road at the time in question and saw the prisoner near Mr. Chorley's warehouse, behaving in an indecent manner He afterwards went into Buttermarket-street. Witness foltowed and heard him make use of foul expressions. Prisoner then struck out right mad iefr, with his stick, and struck the boy Lester a violent blow across the face with it. —John Lestsr, a boy, said that the prisoner without provoca- tion struck him across the face with his stick.—P.C. Stuart spoke to seeing the assault on Lester.—z4ergeant Bramley, from Orford Barracks, stated that the prisoner was in a militia regiment. He should have been serving at the front but at the time the regiment departed he was an ahsentee.—The Chief Constable Not an absent-minded beggar. but absent in bady. (Lauehter )—The h rgeant, oonttnuing. said the man has a very bad chatacter He Issd committed four crimes this year.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. A Susototoue CHARACTER.—WiIIiam Oldham of no settled abode. was charged with being found on the enclosed pre- mises of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company at Dallam with latent to commit a felony at two o'clock that morning.—Henry Lloyd, night watchman stated that he found the prisoner behind a waggon. He questioned him and he said he was '* after work." He further stated that he had only got some old hoops and he put those back again. A robbery of a serious nature was committed between Friday night and Saturday morning and he believed that the prisoner was in the forge on Friday. - Prisoner, against whom five previous appearances had been recorded, Was committed to gaol for three months. FIGHTING.—Fer committing a breach of the neace by fighting in Golden Grove on the 13t.h April Thomas Knockton 22. Dial-street and Thomas Sauce, 9. Croppers Brow were bound over to keep the peace. Knocktoa being ordered to pay full costs (7.) and Sauce half casts. SILVER SQUaIIIC Irf IN UPRoAL—Blirabeth Kearns, Wm. Rankin far d Sarah Jane Rankin, residing in Silver Square Were summoned for committing a breach of the pe ice by act- ing in a disorderly manner in Shier Square on April 14th.— Annie Doulan, Ellen Roberts and Michael CorLett living in the same neighbourhood were charged with making use of obscene language at the same time and place.—P.U. Turner proved the ease and stated that Silver Square was in an up- roar for about half an hour,—Mr Birchen : Is it ever any- thing else.—Doulan it wa, stated by the Chief Constable.bad been before the magistrates ten times, Kearns 16 times and Roberts 7 times.—These defendants were fined 5s and costs (12s) and the others Tis each. FURIOUS CYCLING.—Arthur Gilmore. 129, Longford-street was summoned for furiously riding a bicycle in Lovely•lane on the 12th April.—PO. Turner stated that he saw the defendant cycling along Lovely-lane in the direction of Folly Lane at a furious rate. He shouted to him to stop but he would net. A little further on he fell off the machine. He gave a wrong • name and address when told ha should be re- ported. He had lost 'his pedals.—Fined 5s FURIOUS PRIVING.—Thomas B rerall, 37, Crossley-street was summoned for furiously driving a horse and cart in Lovely-lane on the 16th April.—P.O. Cooner stated that the defendant drove at the rate of at least 12 miles an hour.— Fined ss. DISORDICRLY rioNDUCT.—john Ward and Thomas Birks were bound over to keep the neme and fined in the costs for having committed a breach of the peace by acting in a dis- orderly manner in Churck-street on April 16th.

A SERIOUS OFFENCE —William Parker was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and tarry in [dam- street at 11.10 on 'Won illy morning.—? C. Plumb said he saw the prisoner sitting on the front of the turn. He was under the influence of drink and witness on getting him oil the vehicle found he could scarcely stand.—The Chief Consr.able' said the lurry was laden with carboys containing carbolic acid. A fine of 5& and costs was imposed. WEDNEID AM—Before Alderman Sutton (in the chair), and _ .
Messrs. Geddes and Birchall,

Napier-street was charged with • stealing from the shop of Isaac Hougtten, pawnbroker, Mersey-street a pair of men's mole trouser's of the value of ss.—The Chief Constable stated that at 10.30 on Monday Mr. Houghton's son saw, the trousers safe on a chair on the outside of the counter. He subsequently missed them and information was given to the Pollee. On Tuesday morning Detective Meaceek ascertained that the trousers had been plesiged by the prisoner at a pawnshop in Dial-street. Prisoner was arrested and admiGted the offence.—As it was prisoner's first off snag the manfs rates took a lenient view of the case and fined her lOs with the option of 7 days,' imprisonment.

WARRINGTON 'BUS DRIVER Ft:gm—Samuel Williams 'bus driver, in the employ of Mr. Blew," Connor, was summoned for leaving a 'bus at itackton Heath on April 14th.—He pleaded not guilty.—P.S. Bourne stated that the defendant was the driver of e'bus which ran between Stockton Heath and Warrington. On the evening of April 14th he saw the defendant driving a 'bus in the Old London•road and he stopped and left it near the aquare. There was a good amount of traffic about, and once the ho see started end had to be stopped by a passenger. The 'bus was there from 6.25 to 6 45. He found the defendant in the Mulberry Tree Hotel having his tea. He was rather advanced in A similar occurrence to3k place a few days before this. De- fendant said the guard was in etierge of the 'eus. He was on duty from 8 a.m. until 11 p.m. and had to have his meals in the 'bus, but when there were passengers in the 'bus he had to have them at a public-house —The Chairman in fining the defendant 5s said it was a very dangerous peactice aid in future such cases would in the interests of the publie be very severely dealt with.
