div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
RUNCORN VICTORIOUS TO THE END.
Champions Beat the Rest.
Presentation of the Cup.

Runcorn as an academy for Northern Union Rootballers has proved its crialitiss in unmistakable fashion during the season just concluded. fhrougheut their perform- ances have been consistent and brilliant. Plevieg secured the greatest majority of points le ths Lancashire section, of the Northern Union, Runcorn secured for themselves for the second time in five years possession of the ' magnificent cup the premier club are allowed to hold for twelve months as a recognition of their prowess. When Runcorn were an amateur team purely,their task of showing superiority was a much easier one; but in latter years monied clubs have been able to import 531113 magnificent talent from Scrath Wales and elsewhere, so that the struggle of purely local teams has been a chequered one. Runcorn proudly—though some ',multi have us believe through poverty—have adhered to thsir own sons for the muscle and &new that should van- quish all in the Football Arens, and as events have proved have done so not in vain. But to continue, another priv ?lige gained by Runcorn as the resultant of their winning the championship was the honour of entertaining the rest of the league on their own ground, to an exhibition game. The event proved highly inter- esting and though the day was far too hot for the winter sport to be seen at its beat, there have been many games during the past season that lacked, by a long way the interest, incident ani excitement that charac erissd this, the chief event of Saturday. There was a large crowd present when the teams lined out as under, and the Irwell-lane enclosure, bethe I as it was in soft warm sunshine never looked better : Runcorn: Houghton, back ; Jones, J Butterworth, Warder, and 0 Butterworth. three-quarter back,. ; J Jolley, and Faulkner, half backl; Walker, Farmer, Tom- linaon,Reece, Lightfoot,Leogley, Derlingson and Hughes forwards. Rest of League: Rieg (Rochdale Hornets), back; Bown (Widnes), James (Broughtoe Rangers), Hodgson (Stockport), and Wightman (Rochdale Hornets), three- quarter basks ; .Lawtnn and Lees (Oleham), half backs ; Ellis and Moffat (Oldham), Thompsen (Broughton Rangers), Frater (Oldham), Simister (Stockport), Aspey (Widnes), Winskilt (Broughton Ringers), and Briers (S.. Helens) forwards. Touch judges: Messrs. J. Underwood and E. Gresty; referee : Mr. J. Priestly. The rest commenced hostilities, and for a time thair dash was irresistible, and the home team were forced open the defensive. James proved clever and fast, and he was atly seconded by flown. Things were exceed- ingly lively. To add to Runcorn's discomfiture Jolley got his finger dislocated and was forced to retire. Run- corn's defence was now subjected to a fine concerted attack, but Houghton, Butterworth, Warder, and Wilkinson showed a united trent that brooked not defeat: Their defence was a feature in itself. Jolley shortly after returned, and imna idiately his well-known figure was seen at work. The ball came out to be secured by him, and a fine passing bout was commenced. How the home crowd did yell when its final mutt saw J. Butterworth lying prone upon the oval on the other side of the" Rest's" line. Farmer added to the enjoy- ment by kicking straight and five points were soon up. Then followed some txceedingly bright passages from both sides, the forwards and backs indulging in some real good passing. Jolley diversified a little by dropping a goal. The visiters hooked a little down their noses at this ; and made futile but magnificent attempts to re- gain some of their waning prestige. No go, however, Runcorn were the best, and would not be denied. At- tacking for the first time in deadly earnest,Joßey started seine more passing. Faulkner helped it on, others were there ready and willing to add to the sport, and subse- quently 0 Butterworth getting possession he made use of a fine opening and secured a try. This point was not converted. Play continued of a high order on to the interval which arrived with Runcorn 10 points, (2 goals 2 tries) ; to rest of competitors, nil. The second half of the game WAS a bright, exhilarat- ing one. Sometimes the advantage was with the " Rest." then again with Runcorn. Rigg was always busy, and so too was Houghton for that matter, but the defence of both sides was good. kspey proved a busy forward. but Farmer and Walker of Runcorn were oft-times busier. The backs of both teams were shadows to one another,and each one's via a via never got far before being grassed. A finely contested half was concluded without any addition to the score, but all the players gained in the estimation of the spectators, for none played badly and some superbly. The final result was a well earned victory for Runcorn by 10 points to nil.

-THE PRESENTATION OF THE CUP. A High Compliment to Runcorn. A Nursery for Footballers. The match over the large crowd surged around the front of the grand stand where the cup was on view upon a temporary stand covered with green cl ith. In- side the enclosure were Messrs J Underwood (president of the Lancashire Section), S Taylor, J.P. (president of the Runcorn F.C.) ; several members of the R.F.C. Com- mittee, including Messrs W Jones (chairman), J Eulson (secretary), C Pownall (treasurer), A Lightburn, etc. ; captain S Houghton, and the members of his team ; Mr Howett (of Northwich), Superintendent D Pearson (of the Runcorn Police), etc. Mr 1 Underwood as president of the Lancashire section of the Northern Union Competition, said he might Fay he was very pleased to come that afternoon and prwent the handsome cup before them to the Runcorn ',cam for their meritorious performance during the season. (Hear hear.) Most of them would think with him it had been too hot that day for football, but all kinds of weather had to be put up with, and that was one of the difficu:- ties with which Runcorn had had tocontend with during the season, which was another reason why he should say their performance had been a meritorious one. (Applause). Again they had gone right through the season and only lost two matches- (Appleuse). It was, he repeated, a most meritorious performance (hear, hear, and loud applause.) He was sure the people af Runcorn ought to be delighted with their team.—(A Voice: We are.)—(Lod applause.) They ought to be! They ought to be ! For he believed every member of the team was a native of the town or district. —(cheers)—which was a very strong point, in hi mind. They were locals purely.—(Voice: We have more yet ) (Cheers.) Be was sure they had a thorough good nursery for footballers. They seemed to know how to rear and =earth them, for they always had a fresh lot ready when the others were worn out. (Loud applause.) He was sure they would all be delighted to see their cap- tain receive that cup—(hear, hear, and applauae)—and he had very great pleasure indeed in asking Mr. Bough- ton to accept the cup. (Applause) Having taken a drink out of the cup, Mr. Underwood then handed it over to Captain Hsugliton, and the band struck up " See the Conquering Here." Mr. S Houghton thanked Mr. Underweod on behalf of himself and tee team for the kind manner in which he had treated the players.—Mr. Houghton's speech was received with uproarous cheering. Mr. Underwood then produced the medals the differ- ent members were entitled to, and presented the lot to; Mr. S. Taylor, the presideet of the Runcorn club, to accept for the team.

Mr. S. Taylor who was received with quite an ovation said it gave him extreme pleasure to thank Mr. Under- wood on behalf of the Runcorn Football Club and all interested. As could be seen from the happy counten- ances la,fore them it gave everyone great pleasure to see Mr. Underwood present carrying out a duty—in which he tank s ) much pleasure himself—(applause)—the duty of presentir4g the handsome cup and medals to the Runcorn team. They would agree with him that the cup and medals had been most worthily earned. (Hear, hear and applause.) It would be much appreciated by the num,rous persons who toek an interest in the deings of the Runcorn Football Club. (Applause.) He must also tell Mr. Underwood of the extreme pleasure he felt throughout the season to be one of the swctators present at the games that had t iken place on that ground ,games which had baen contested so fairly, so nobly and so gentlemanly. (applause.) He must add a word in favour of the teams which had visited Runcorn during the season. He was sure there was not one which visited the ground that hat] given rise to the slightest , unpleasantness. (Applause.) As Mr. Underwood would !be aware more so than himself that at a time when excitement was at its highest there might have been a little " off Play" still he was sure nothing of the!. kind had been door intentionally by ! ether the Runcorn mea or their visitors (Loud applause.) He again thanked Mr, Underwood for the kind way in which he had expressed himsel: and pr ,sented the cup and medals, (Cheers.)

Mr. W Jones, Chairman of the RF C. Clmmittee, moved a hear.:y rote of thanks to Mr. Underwood for presenting the cup and medals to the team. He hoped it would not be the Is time—it was the second— (cheer)—that Mr. Underwood would officiate there. (Renewed cheers.) They were to have another chance, and as long as they had Vie class of men they had that day it would not be a bad one. (Applause.) The vote wag accorded mo3t heartily.

Mr Underwood ht ackbOvided.ting the vote, said he had only done what was a very pleasant duty to him. (Applause ) Mr. Hewett (of Messrs. Bwrn, Thompson and Corn- panv),then deliv.,red a short address in which he laugh- ingly moved A vote of thank, to Mr. S. Taylor, whom he said was dying to get it. In fact he had sat by Mr. Taylor ,-,nd he had ickl him into gettin7 on ha feet to m )vm that, vote of thanks which he wanted to take home in his p,'cket. (Loud laughter.) Having paid a high compliment to the Runcorn Foottall Team which h? describe .l as the best on earth Mr. Hewett added he hoped the club would go 03 prospering and bring the cup a third time to Runcorn.
The vite of thanks to Mr. Taylor was carried with accla.ma Mon.

Subsequently Captain S Houghton, cqrrying the cup, and eqcorted by the othpr waren ot the tun, was pre- rid by the Band nf the 2nd Earl Cheshire Volunteer Flattilion, playing "We beat tem onc,3 before boys," to the dresqing roornq a', the Wilson Hotel.
rho whole scene was a very thrilling and enthusiastic one.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. ---- LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. ---- LANCASHIRE LEAGUE.
Earlestown v. Wigan County.

Beautiful weather favoured the visit of Wiqn County to the MIAPPEIoe Ssturday and it wag surprising to find only about 500 spectat4rs turn out t 9 witness the match. Perhaps it was the hest and the counter attraction of a cricket match at Nswton tha-. kept the majlrity away as the day was far mire su,t,i for cricket than football. The ho:nesters were fully represented, Sharratt appear- ing at right outside in olsce of Elarrkon. The visitors waved the scratch team,that is completing their fixtures and soon after hill-past three th 3 teams faced as fell iws

Eerlestown : Chew. goal ; Heyes and Cotton, backs ; Pennington Green and Clibborn half-backs ; Sharratt, Whitehouse, Ellis, Lnach and Settle, forwards. Wigan County : Savage., goal ; Cook and Sudworth, hacks ; Hari,Postlethwaite and Holden half-back ;Birch, Dean, Evans, Watson, and Cawley, forwards. The visitors won the toss and they set Earlestown to face the slope and a brilliant sun. Despite these, how- ever, the /rimesters were the first to become dangerous, Set"le and Leach working the ball well into the County half and after a lot of mancaavring Settle got in a shot which hit one of the backs, and meeting the rebound the same player shot yards wide. Borh sets of players seemed to know that there was very little at stake as they took irhines pretty easily and as a consequence neither of the glint-keepers had much to do. A neat pass from Whirehouie gave Sharratt an onening, which he lost no time in turning to account. He obtained the ball near to the half way line and dashing off up the wing was met close in by Sud worth whom he tapped the ball past and folio wine it up drove it into the wit at liglitnine speed. Straight from the centre kick Leach obtained possession and breaking through all opposition he had no difficulty in registering the second point, Savage hav- ing no possible chance of saving either of the two shots which beat him. The County roused up Men these two reverses and for a tiny the exchanges were confined to the borne half. The Earlestowts d 4ence however, was quite equal to all th 3 calle made upon it, toe backs kick- ing as cleanly as possible and the austoiian dealing with all the shots rained in upon him, with ease. Just before the interval Pestlethwaita had a spleedid chance of re- ducing the arrears but with the goal practically at h s mercy, he shot yards toe high. Half time, Eirlestown two; Wigan County. nil. After a rather lengthy refresher the laomesters again took up the running but they were me by a sturdy de- fence and despite the fact that they kept the county almost entirely on the defensive, they could not add to their score, Towards the close the play fell away con aiderably, both sides evidently being done up after their running about under a broiling sun. The finish came with the half time score unaltered and the players thankful at being able to escape the scorching hot sun- Taking the game as a whole, the play was of a very poor character indeed neither team coming anywhere near Lancashire League form. Cnevr was quite safe in the Eerleetown goal and the backs also played a cool sound game. The half- backs were moderate, Pennington being about the beet of this trio. He tackled fearlessly and plac9d the ball to his forwards in splendid fa.shion. Sherratt, the new right outside ia a promising player. and as he is still very young, he ought t / turn out a valuable catch for Earles- town, The visitors' forwards were very ragged, but that is not surprising seeing that they are a scratch lot. the half-hacks and hacks were very Rafe, especially during the second half, when the hernesters werA press- ing them severely. The custodian brought off one or two smart saves, and could not be blamed for the two shots which beat him.

The Clerk was appointed to the chair pre tem —Mr. Garnett stated that owing to ill-health he had bevist ad- vised not to undertake any duties beyond what he was bound to do. Be thanked the members for the courtesy and attention they had given him during his t -rni of office and proposed that Dr. Murray be appointed chair man for the ensuing twelve months.—Mr John Dignum seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously —Mr R Garnett was elected vice-chairman Mr. Clarke proposed that the retiring overseers, Messrs Charles S Parker, J B Aitken, and Dr Murray, be re- elected.—Mr. Garneft stated that Mr Parker was away from home, and far from well. div.head: MARRIED WHEN DYING. ----- And the Sequel!
div.p: MARRIED WHEN DYING. ----- And the Sequel!

A PATEIETIC story, connee.ed with thn devoted attach- ment ot a young married couple living in London, has been published in the " Weekly Dispatch," a reporter on that paper hiving spent an evening with the lady and her husbana at their home, 37, Irene-road, Parson's Green. Mrs. Webb and her husband were by and girl together, went to the same school, and played side by side.

"We were very fond of each other "said Mrs. Webb, "even in those days.and he was always ready to protect me, because I was not half as robust acid strong as other girls. Somehow it seemed to be understood that when we grew up we should be married; but, as we grew older, I could see that my future was likely to be a sad one. I came of a doomed family. My father died of consump- tion at forty, and of the nine sans and daughters six died of consumption, am I one of my brothers is almost dying now. It was stated that I should never live to see five-and-twenty, and, remember, this came from one of the best physicians in England. le ever a woman lived a living death, I did. In the winter it was impossible for me to go out, and when I did go backwards and forwards to Brompton Hospital for Con- sumptives, it used to take me hours and hours to walk even a few hundred yards. When I coughed I felt as if two great strings inside me were tearing my very heart out. At night I lay shivering in bad with horrible per- spirations, and I felt as if death would be welcome. k: took me hours to dress, and at least half an hour to get dawn a short eight of stairs. Th!'r&'s a photograph I had taken just before we were mauled, and, as you can see, my friends spoke the truth when they said that if I had had a piece of white round my face I should have looked exactly as if I had been laid out.' "As for eating, that was impossible. If I had even a cup of tea it usect to lie on my chest just like a log. One minute I would feel starved, but directly I saw food I did not want it. Mr. Webb had then enlisted in the Durham Light Infantry, and I thought that I should never live until he had servsd his time."

"Let me say a word here," observed Mr. Webb. "Every 's ord my wife says is true. But I had made up my mind to marry her, and I did. I thought she would have died two years before, and on the day of our marriaee my people told me I was marrying a dying woman. Whilst I was in the Army leaved a very decent little amount each year, so that when I had finished my time I had £lOO to my credit. I got a little home together, and we determined to get married. You should have seen her that day. All the way to the church she was leaning on the shoelder of her brother. 6ho was coughing and stopping every few ards—in fact, it was not walking to church, it was crawling there. Week by week she went from bad to worse. I sent her to a specialist, but beyond charging me a very heavy fee he did nce.hine. Then we com- menced buying everything we could hear or read of. That cnpb iard there is filled with medicine bottles. By the time we had been married three years, I had spent the £lOO I had saved on doctors' medicine. It us d nearly to break my heart to see her curlcd up coaching and suffering." " At last a friend suggested that I should try Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people ; I had little hope, for we had tried everything, and found it '.'as only wasting good money, but I bought a box, and she bagan to im- prove after it was finished. Her appetite was better, and the cough not so bad. Then the perspiration stopped and her breathing improved. Alter the fourth box she could get about and actually walked upstairs without stopping. She got stouter, and in pace of her pale sunken cheeks she had a much plumper face. We went on with Dr. Williams' pink pills, and after she had taken them for three months, I found her actually doing her washing sad running up and down the stairs singing she was strong enoueh even to go to a bali. So well did she get that I proposed to the Wesleyan Insurance Company ; that I should take out a policy of insurance on ner life and after an examination she was passed by the doctors She is also insured 'n the Sens ot Temperance Benefit Society, and in all she has been examined by three or four (lectors. lam proud of this beeause it shows me that she must have entirely recovered. lam as happy as a man could possibly be. We are poorer by the loss of the money I took years to save, but I am richer by thousands in having my wife here strong and well and not lying in her erave." Consumption is often thought to be incurab'e, but that is not to say that it ie incurable at every stage ; nor is every case, pronounced by doctors incurable with ordinary medicine, beyond hope, if Dr. Williams' pink pills for pole people, which are not erdinary medicine, ere used. They have cured many cases by replacing the lost blood and increasing the resistant power of the lungs. While even fatal diseases like consemptiou have been repeatedly cured by teem, it is not surprisink that, by enriching the blond sunply, nese pills can cure more common compleints. They are a true tonic, a safeguard against iefluenza and a cere for itr effects ; rheumatism, neuralgia, bronchitis, skin ereptions. and even paralysis yield to the genuine pills, which always bear the full name in seven. woide—Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people:the Tamed price is two shillings and ninepence a box ; substitutes, which never cure, should be avoided.

div.head: Pretoria Arsenal.
div.p: Pretoria Arsenal.
Ten Workmen Killed and Thirty- Two, Injured.
'PRETORIA, WEDNESDAY.

A gc3at explosion occurred last night in Messr-. Begbie and Co.'s engineering works, which ar,.. used as a Government arsenal,under the direction of Herr Gruenberg. The outer walls of the buildings were blown down, and the whole place and neighbour- hood were speedily amass of flames. Che !Wise of the xplosion was terrific, and he shrieks of the women and children in the adjoining streets added to the horror of the_scene. Ten workmen were killed and thirty-two wounded. Herr Gruenberg was slightly injured. It is stated that the most important part of the machinery was saved.

More Militia to be Embodied. Orders having teen revived for the embodiment of the 6th (late 4th) battalion Sings Liverpool Regiment, the members of the Battalion wfa assemble at Orford Barracks, Warrington, on May 3rd at 8 am. From thenee they will proceed tl Fermoy, Ireland, where they will be stationel until further ordefs.

div.head: WARRINGTON VOLUM rEERS FOR
div.p: WARRINGTON VOLUM rEERS FOR
THE FRONT.

Swearing-in Ceremony. For the third time, the Mayor of Warrington has been called upon to witness the attestation ot local Volunteers, who with true patriotism have COMB forward in the hour of their country's need and offered themselves for active service in South Africa. Monday evening was the time chosen for the swear- ing-in of the twenty volunteers who are with Lieu- tenant Carey to form the draft which is to recruit the, ' volunteer company connected with the Ist South Lancashire Regiment now in Natal. Tee large audience which witnessed this interesting ceremony was evidence of the sympathetic interest which is taken in the movement by the public generally. The Mayoress and several other ladies graced the proceedings with their presence, and among others present were Lieutenant-Colonel Itidgway,Major Roome (adjutant),Captain Hutchin- son, V.D., Captain J D Fairclough, Captain B Fair- clough,Lieutenants 51edley,Robert5 and Williamson Quartermaster Potter. Sergeant-Major Rawlinson, Mr J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Councillors Bennett, John 'Roberts, Rogers, James Nvans, Jehn Evans, Smethurst, Peacock, Lee, Baird, Heaton,and S Davies. The twenty men who were to be attested paraded in drill order with kersey frocks and fi. Id service cps. They were drawn up in front ot the table at which the Mayo, was seated. Other volunteers without uniform stood to attention in single file down two Rides of the hail • A large concourse of people witnessed the 1 ro- dedings from the bottom of tee hall. Colonel RIDGWAY said he was please I to see the man there as the number chosen to go out to join the 40:e in Fckutla Africa. tie was particularly pleased when be thought that their battalion had been chosen to send out the first section. (Applause.) They had done well before in sending out a number of men larger than they expected and he was very proud that such a number had come forward to do their duty towards their Queen and country. (Applause.) They all wished they might come safely through the South African campaign, and he was quite sure that they would do their bast. They knew now what the 40th had done, and what it had gone through. They had felt the very sad toes of their dear old friend, Colonel O'Leary, an officer who when he was adjutant in Warrington every man respected and be (Colonel Ridgway) thought also every man lowd. (Hear, hear.) Be knew that all the officers who knew him did. His death was a great loss to the regiment, and they in Warrington had lost a dear and sincere friend. They would ever remember him by the present of the shield be made to them, and he trusted that every man who went in And tried to win that shield would have a greater interest in it for the reason that it had beert given to them by an old friend. (Hear, bear.) The Mayer. 'who would attest them, was extremely kind to show Buell an interest in the corps. They. all knew what he hid done for them in the past, and they hoped he would do what be coald in the future. (Applause.) The men then took the oath of allegiance. At the con- elusion' of the ceremony, The MAYOR, who was cordially received, said : Ser- geant Wbitfield and men. On behalf of my fel:ow townsmen, and on my own behalf, it affords me the 1 greatest possible pleasure to express to you, the warm' admiration we feel for that patriotism which has led you to offer yourselves for active service in Suth Africa. (Hear, hcar.e On two previous occasions', it has been nil- honourable privilege to speak in similar terms to those who have left us. aad are already serving our be- -104 Qeeen, and helping to maintbin the' prestige of our army at the fe*t. (Applause.) Now that the ex- cicement and erithasiasm which was at first evoked by the criminal folly of President Kruger in declaring war arakiast•the Britistrnation has had time to abate, and a we have all had innumerable opportunities, although in onlya remote fashion,of realisiug the hardshipetrials,tee horrible privationeend terrible bloodshed which has foe lowed,it is quite evideut,ehat the spirit which has animate you can only be that spirit which has drawn to us from all the Colonies Of our Empire the countle.e4 multitedes of' men, kindred to us in blood end in all those glorious tedieitions, which whereVer our lag has flown have led to the exticnsienotfeeedoin and* justice, and to the due re9ognition. of. equal rights to all men. (Applause.) I trust it may not be necessary for me to act again in tots capacity, becausel believer that the ability of Lord Rqberts end those wilo have the honour to serve ueder a) command—in ' spite of the temporary; shall I say h illation of sornsfeeet -those gine generals which has co e about by the, unnecessary publication of Lord R erts'sdeppeeehes concernirig them, a criticism which might well'i ave been het&over until. the conclusion of MI war-e(applause)—end the magnificent force of fight. in . men now 'awaiting. or carrYing out his orders, is eeseal to ail the dernends. whinh may be • made upon' tillmt iSee +Whether I am right In this assirription. or not, thik.keio ksieve, that w„hateyer demands may be .made uesellitheeeitbeeler res.+ a lel to equipment, money, or men, the loyalty of the people of Warrington to the Queen, whom we venerate and oisr determination that the glorious heritage of Empire upon which we have entered should be handed down to our children more firmly established than ever before, will enable us to meet those demands with chat spirit which has always character- ized the British nation in its hour of trial. (Applause.) It now only remains for me to add that we all most fer- vently hope that this war may be speedily brought to a successful issue, and that you may safely return to US, in cenananY with your gallant comrades who left us only a few short weeks ago. (Applause). Cheers were elven for the Queen, the National Anthem was sung, the band accompanying, and cheers for the Mayor concluded the proceedings.

div.head: Pieter's Hill Fight.
div.p: The Pieter's Hill Fight.

The f ollnwine lttr has been received by Mrs. Conroy. who resides in Asliten—tree!7, Watrioe:on, from her son, Martin Conroy, of the South Lancaohire Reeiment. Tbe letter wes eeclesed in a Queen's chocolat e box : " Pieterm an zburg, March 15-Ai. Dear Mother,— We are at present having a much-needed rest. We have completed a very hard task, that i 3, to relieve Ladysmith—a thing we have been fiethine for since we arrived out here. Tnis is the third ddlerent way we have tried to get to Ladysmith, first at Spion Kop, then at Petgieter's Drift, and finally this way, which wa3 the turning key ot the war, and it was a gr.d. send I'on those in Ladysmith for US to arrive when we did, for they were starving. They were living, tin one biscuit and a bit of horseflesh a day. It was a grand sight the day we relieved it, far better than any jubilee or festival. We commenced by advancing on the evening of February 14th. Fern then until March Ist, we drove them from, hill to hill, never letting: them rest night or day. It is all very well for people to sit at home and criticize our geeerals' work, and say they would do this and that, but if they had the faintest ' idea of the positioas we had to tackle they would be of a different opinion. Had we been in the same positions all the armies in the world would not drive us out of them. Our hardest battle was on the 27ch February. It is a great day amongst the Boers, it is the anniversary of Majuba, and in their way they were going to give U 3 a hot time, but we turned the tables. As we advanced up Pieters Hill the Boers sent a hail of bullets down upon us. but we crept alone, then fixed our bayonets, and with a ringing cheer we rushed into their trenches. They fired on until we got within 50 yards, and then they . threw down their rifles for mercy, a few of them were taken prisoners, but it was our officers who stopped us killing the lot of them. lam very sorry to say that whilst our Colonel was leading us up the hill he was killed. Everyone in the regiment liked him, and plenty were moved to tears when we buried him next morning. As you will see,the box is empty, and not as I promised. The reason is, we captured a hill from the Boers and they had a hill opposite to us, and it was almost certain death to anyone to come near us ; 90 as we ceu!d not ge, anything to eat we ate our chocolate. It was very lucky we had it. I hope all are in good health at borne as lam in perfect health. Kindly remember me to all I know With the help of God, we .11‘11 annn he returning."

The 6th Battalion Liverpool Regiment under command of Colonel C. C. Woodward will assemble at Warrington next Thursday and will as already indicated go to Ireland to be stationed at Farmoy. The 3rl Bot;:alion Cneshire Regiment commanded by Colonel A Hill will be embodied at Caester on Thursday and go to Aldershot for the training. Lieutenant Delrnage, 6th Battalion Liverpool Regitn-nt at Warrington has been appointed second lieutenant in the re zular cavalry and joins the 21,t Lancers now at Curragh camp in Ireland. He jsinel the 6th Battalion Liverpool Regiment in July 1897. Lieutenant Wilmer, of the sth Battalion Liverpool Regiment,has also been appointed second lieutenant in the Scottish Rifles Iliad joins the 2ad battalion of the corps. He was anointed to the militia battalion at Warrington in February of last year. Lieutenant Canyon has been formally promoted Captain in the South Lancashire Regiment and appointed to command a company in the first Battalion in South Africa. He joine I tae R,egiment in October 1890. Lieutenant Colonel Honwold will temporarily command the Lancashire Hussars during toe train- ing Colonel Lord Gerard being ab4ent in South Africa. Colonel the Earl of Harrington of the Cheshire Yeomanry also replaces Lord Gerard as chief of the 9th Yeomanry Brigade which con-ists of the Lancashire Hussars and the Cheshire Yeo- manry. Colonel Howel Gunter. who lately gave up com- mand of the local forces in gleensianl, hes taken over command of the 63rd (Manchester) Regimen- tal diarict, and will also act as commandant of the Nlanchester Volunteer Infantry Brigade, Lieutenant Barnes who lately resigned his posi- tion in the old Royal London Militia has been ap- pointed Captain in the .sth battalion Liverpool Re.:iment with headquarters at Warrington, and he has joined that corps at Dublin where it is now temporarily located. Captain Mason has been promoted Major in the first Cheshire Volunteer Artillery, becoming the junior field officer of the corps, He joined the brigade in 1887, becoming criptain in 1891.

div.head: LATE CATAiti DAVIES
div.p: THE LATE CATAiti DAVIES
Sketch of • His Life.

The mortal remains of the late Captain Edward Davie' were laid in their last resting place, in Runcorn Ceme- tery, on Saturday afternoon last. Tne town displayei many manifestations of regret, and the river Mersey was a sight to behold a;mest every craft, from a skiff to an ocean-going steamer fly-in; its calonea at half-mast. 'I he coffin which was of solid oak alai fitted with bras i mountings was first ret al: borne into St. Johns Presby- terian Chapel,Vietoria-road,where the Rev Sydney Morris (pastor) performed the first portiere of tie burial aervic The coffin was then transferred to the hearse an pro ceedcd by York-street, and Green re .a-road to the Genie tery. At the graveside the Rev S Morris, concludel the burial service. The following is an interesting sketch of the late Captain Edward D ivies's career:—Bern in Manchester in the year 1.830, he commenced work at the very early age of seven years as half timer in a cotton factory it. , half day at work and half day at a school cennected with the factory. After staying a short time he entered the service of a drysalter, as office boy, and remained there until his parents removed t 3 Liverpool, ta which town he accompanied them and was sent to Mr Cropper's school at the Dingle. After leaving school, he get employment in several shops And was. able. to he ejapprenticed to aMr LLoYd...grocer, Victestl'Ot,‘chen his father died, and he returrird with hi imither t) Manchester. Not feeling emitent at Manchester, he jeurneyed to Runcorn and got employment at a shop in Bridge-street, a,nd afterwards shipped- as boy or board a Bridgewater Trustee Float (this was oa the 19. th Jane, 1847). After a time he was prom.ted to the Swift boats which carried passengers between Mane-14er aril Runcorn, covering the distance of 3'3 miles in 31 hours. Some time after the Swift bolts ceased running he joined one of the Bridgewater Trustees Steamers employed on the River Mersey'. between Liverpool and Riancorn. In January 1858 he to-la coal mand of the steamer " Blanch," then carry- ing passengers between the above two, towns On the Ist March 1860 he was appointed Deck and Pier Master at Dukes Dock Liverpoel. On Decem- ber Ist 186 i, be was aapointed superintendent of the Bridgewater Trustees Steamers,Liehthonses, Lightships, and Buoying Zaz-, of the Upper Mersey, which position he held until January let, 1877, when ii-Bciard of Com- missioners having. been formed for the purpose of Light lag and Buoying Sze, of the Upper Mersey he was ap- Pointed:bv them as.srap,erintendent of the said Llghting, Bitoaing-ike, which porition he held until the time of his death. During his career he etiperintended the raiaing of twenty eight sunken craft (stearriiirs". and flats), all of which were successfully, floated and he was alsfa engaged in a number of other salvage dutiee. From June lth 1882, to May 7ch.1863, he superintended the transaip ment of cargo from the Steam ship " Great Eastern "to fiats at New Ferry, on her several voyages from New York. . div.head: TEM CUOICE OF CHAIRII&N.

Mr. S. Jeacock prop aed that. Mr James Looker ba the chairman of the Council for the ensuing year. Tday all knew him and were acquainted with hi long connection with the parish. whin dated from the days of the Burial Board. Tney always found Mr Looker most satisfactory and regular in his attendacce3, and he (the speaker) did not think they could get a better chairman. Therefore, he had great pleasure in proposing him. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Hulme seconded with equal pleasure, and the re- solution was carried most unanimously. Mr. Looker said he thanked them all very much for the kind words which they had used in epeakin; of him. He had always tried—during the last 18 years—whilst on the Burial Board and in all his pablic work to do his duty, for the parish of Halton. (Hear, hear.) Looking back anon his predecessors in the chair he coald not but feel that the Council had conferred a very great honour upon him by electing him to the post. Whilst in office he had endeavoured to do his duty both to the Council and to the rat!payers in general. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.)

_ THE ASTNIOOR BRIDGE. Mr. Robert Hughes observed there was nothing in the minutes of the last meeting with regard to the Astmoor Bridge. At the last Parish Council meeting it vas given as understood, by the Chairman, that the Council should hear something about the buildirie from Mr. Stokes. He should like to ask whether there was anyth'ne said, or whether any information had been gathered as the result of the letters the Clerk had ben instructed to write? Had tbe CJuncil received any replies in any shape or form? Mr. Jeacock also vieed the Clerk whether any com- munication had been receivei from the County Council wile regard to the Aetenoor Bridge? lie be,ieved there was some correspondence—and he had seen in print though not in the p abli prees—where it was stated that the matter would bs referred to the P-1.1 Council of Haltsn. If the c ranunie ition had come to the Clerk, he Mt they could deal with it. The Clerk replied that no communication had been received from the Council respeeting the subject under discussion. Mr. Jeacock then suggested that should the Clerk receive any co.ninunication he should call a "meeting at once. Mr. Robert Hueltee rather favoured a courseof writing to the County Csuncil asking what steps had ben taken in the matter. They would then be sure of a reply ad something to work on. Talking generally, several nsembers observed it was their opinion that the subject had been knocked in the head. It would never come to anything whilst there was the obstacle in the way there appeared to be. In Fact, the County Cauncil, were determined not to go on with the matter, because of the fearful sum that was asked for the land. Mr. Robert Hughes expressed a desire to know more about the obstacle. The Chairman thought it woald be beat to let the matter lie over. Mr. Hughes: Ido not think so. Mr. Jeacock said he knew the price asked for the land but as the matter was so far private he would no'! divulge it. The subject of the road, however, was more for the County Council than for them, and he proposed that the course he suggested be taken, and that they do nothing in the matter until it was referred to them. Mr. Ackerley seconded, and the resolction was carried nein con.

T3E TRIALS OF AN OVERSEER. Mr. Robert Hughes proposed that Messrs. S Jeacock and 3 Ackerley be re-eircted overseers. Mr. S Barow seconded. Ackerley; I rather propose lam going to resign. uglii ter.) Mr. Jaacuck too would like the Council to look for another one, to take Ws place. The post of overseer was a very remunerative one —(laueht,r)—and had a large says, attached to it in the shape of a great deal of abuse and (R neswe I laughter.) He did not t link there would possibly have been any or abuse in connection with toe office,especially when a person tried to discharge the duties of overseership fairly ber.ween man and man. (Hear, hear.) Mr Jeacock here related some of thb unpleasantries of his office and how he had been soundly abuied by some persons who considered they had not been fairly dealt with in the way of estimates. In concluding Mr Jeacock said he didn't want to be the recipient of this abuse any longer, and consequently would be glad to be relieved of the over- seership. Mr. Ackerlev took the same view as Mr. Jeacock and endorsed all he bad said. The Chairman was of the opinion that they could not get two better overseers. (Hear, hear.) He hoped, therefere, they would see their way Zo take the office once &spit]. He knew that public work hail that pecu- larity about it that it was never said te be well done. There was always some little obstacles in the Way, still he did hope they would take the office again. (Ap- plause.) Mr. W. Moore said in his opinion it would be a very serious loss to the p keel of Halton if the two gent'emen could not be prevailed upon to again take office. Ile had no doutt what they had said was quite true, and that I they were subject to ill will and abuse. He had not come across the man yet who could do his duty in a Public office fairly between man and man, without having to put up with some abuse. Still he was sure that abuse erninated from unprincipled men. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that Mr. Jeacock and Mr. Ackerley would not think for a moment that the abuse of those few was the opinion of the ratepayers of Halton gener- ally. It would be a great loss to Halton if they declined the post. so, he hoped they would try again. (Hear, hear and applause.) Mr. Barrow : Yes, try ae,ain ! Mr. Jeacock then said if Mr Ackerley was willing to, they would tr.? again. (Hear. hear.) Referring to the work of assessment Mr Jeacock said the assessing of workmen's cottages was all right, they were assessed to their full rent. With the larger properties however, it was different. Ho was told, however, there was going to be an alteration. The project was to employ a com- petent man who would go around valuing all the pro- perties in the union. That would te taking the responsi- bility off the overseers, who were not always competent to value property in every case. They knew how to value cottages for it was known in the street how the workmen were paid, but the valuation of railways, gas works, gas mains, water mains and such things were beyond ordinary men like himself. It would he A valuable addition to the union if an engineering gentle- man, and one 'nil versed in these matters, made a fair valuation ,throughout the union. For he did believe there were great anomalies not only in the rate book of Halton, but in the rate books throughout the union, therefore the district council would be well advised to employ a man of that description. (Hsar, hear.) Subseepently, both Mr Jeacock and Mr Ackerley con- sented to act for a further term, and were unanimously re-alected.

div.head: DEATH OF THE EX-MAYOR OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: DEATH OF THE EX-MAYOR OF WARRINGTON.

The people of Warrington heard with deep regret on Wednesday, of the death at Southport. of the ex-Nlayor,Alderman John Edward Wright, J.P. The sad intelligence was telegraphed to the Mayor, by one of the deceased geatleman'e sons, who stated that his father had passed away peacefully at 10.55. The fleg at the Town Hall was immediately hoisted to half-mast, and the political clubs followed the example imoascliately afterwards. By the death of Alderman Wright, Warrington has not only lost one of the foremost of her self-made eons, but a useful public man. Of late years, Mr Wright has noG en- joyed good health. A few days after the caucus meeting of the Council, at which he was unanimously selected as Mayor for 1893 9, he was suddenly stricken down with haemorrhage in connection with one of the dental vessels and it was feared that his decision to accept office for a second year would have to be reconsidered on account of his illness. Fortunately, he speedily recovered and in Novem- ber last he completed two years of good work as chief magistrate of the town. Since h vacated the position his health again gave grave cause for anxiety. It was in the hope of recruicing it that on the day preceding. Good Friday he proceeded to Seiitkport In Company With. -the- members of his family for a brief sojourn. So receutly as last -Thuteeley he-paid is filing visit to Wareington and re- -turned to Sou' hp irt the same day.On gaturday,ho • ere-r-lso. was-so unwell that a. medical.gentliman- was called in He was found to be suffering from pneu- monia and was immediately ordered to bed. ikon- chitis and congestion of the liver supervened and the case became hopeless. Dr. Joseph, of Warring- ten, paid several visits to the patient at Southport, but all efforts proved unavailing and he died at the time already stated on Wednesday morning. He was 0.2 years of age. He was twice married,his first wife bsing Isabella, the youngest daughter of the tare Mr William Hesketh, builder, by whom he had issue three sons and two daughters. His second wife is the eldest daughter of Mr Thomas Birtles,of Sankey-sm)et,who presented him with a son during his Nfayoralty.which was the occasion of a gift of a silver cradle in commemoration of the event from the members of the Cerporation. The deceased gentleman is survived by a widow, three sons and two daughters. Mr. Wright's connection with the Warrington Town Council commenced in he year 1832, wien he was elected as a representative of the South West Ward, succeeding the late Mr. J. P. Wii-• Hams, who had retired. Seven years later, in November 1889, he was elected an Alderman of the ' Borough and continued to hold that position until his death. He was chairman of the Paving and e'ewerage Committee, and a member of the Watch, Street Improvement' Town flail, Park and Baths, Gas, Gymnasium, Parr Hall, Parliamentary, and Tramways Committees. In 1898 he was appointed a representative of the Corporation on the management of the GreenmarSchool. In November 1893,he was elected to the position of Mayor of the Borough and in that capacity he served the town for two years. He took part in a number of impor- tant functions during his Mayoralty, ineluding thel opening of Queen's Gardens and the laying of thel foundation stone of the new constabulary build- ings. He was also called upon to attend many gatherings of a social, ethic ttional and religious character. One act of his stands out conspicuously as an example of his broad-mindedness, and one well calculated to promote religious equality and friendly relations of christian churches. At the Council meting in March, 1898, although a loyal Churchman and closely associated with the Pariah Church and schools, he expressed his intention of attending public worship in Wycliffe Church on the occasion of r.its re-opsnine after renovation% and invited the members of the Council if they were so disposed to accompany kim. The event was unique in the history of Warrington and was a great suc- cess. In 1891. Mr. Wright was appointed a justice of the peace by the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lan- caster, and was very regular in his attendance oe the Borough Bench. A Warriugtonian by birth,Mr, Wright took a deep interest in everything connected with his native town. He was one of those self-made men this town has been proud to possess. He was born near the Paris') Church and at the early age of twelve he commenced work at Howley Saw Mills, which were then owned by Meosrs. J. and P. Worthington. When he had reached his eighteenth year he was articled to tee I ite Alderman John l'ierpoint,archi- tee'', of Bold-street. and four years later he com- menced operations as a builder, which business he successfully carried OR for 15 years, when, owing to a disastrous fire which broke out during the night at his wores in Edgeworth-street, he decided to follow the pro- fession of an architect, surveyor and valuer. He estahlieeed himself in offices in Lyme-street and very speedily made for himself an extensive busi- ness. Latterly his premises have been in Sankey- street and he has had some important work on hand. He was architect for the new works of Messrs. Fletcher, Rus-ell and Company,Limited and for many leading firms in the town. In politics,the deceased gentleman was an ardent Conservative and took an active interest in the organisation of the party. He was a regular attonder at the Parish Church and proved him.elf a useful layman. At one time or other he has filled most if not all the offices which were open to him. Owing to ill-health he asked the last Parish Church vestry to relieve him of the office of sidesman. The schools also claimed his attention and support. Tne remains were brought to Warrington on Thursday evening, - and will be interred in the Cemetery at noon to-day (Saturday). References at the Police Court.

Reference was made at the Borough Police Court on Thursday morning to the death of Alderman Wright. Alderman SUTTON said that before they proceeded to the business of the Court it was his very painful duty to refer to the death of Alderman Wright a member of the Borough Bench of magistrates. he need scarcely say that Alderman Wright would be greatly missed in Warrington. As a magistrate and as an alderman of the borough he had not the slightest hesitation whatever in saying that no man ever devoted himself more and at a greater personal sacrifice to the interests of the town than did Alderman Wright. His death Otin a great loss to the town. Mr. G. F. F. WHITE (magistrates' clerk) on be- half nf his father and himself endorsed the remarks of Alderman Sabi'. During the time Alderman Wright was in health they never had a more regular attendant at court. Mr. Luirg TALEOT (chief constable), on behalf of the police, said the whole force were very deeply shocked when the announcement was made of Alderman Wright's death. As a magistrate and as a member of the Watch Committee he was greatly admired and respected by the police force, and his death would cause a vacancy which it would be difficult to fill.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIATION.
Lord Newton on Home Defence. Conscription Advocated.

The annual general meeting of the Newton Division Coniervative A=sociation was held on Saturday, at the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows. Lord Newton presided, and among a large att.n la.nze were Colonel R Pilkington M.P., Messrs CB F Borron, and Robert Stone (non. treasurers), W Holland Owen (hon. secretary and soliciter),Joha Robinson (Ela.ydock),Alderman Francomb (Warrington), Wyndham isaith (Riaton), W Richardson (Rainford), Thomas Walker (Eceleston), W AMawisley (secretary and agent), Dr: Street, Dr. Handyside, H Barker, J Rudge, acc. Mr. Robinson moved the adoption of the annual re- port and the statement of accounts. Mr. Forshaw secended, and the motion was carried. On the motion ot Mr. Stone, s3concled by Dr. Street, the thanks of the Association were passed to Lord Gerard for his services as president, and he was again elected. Thanks were also given to the bon secretary and bon auditors. Dr. Hanayside and Mr. Borron ware appointA as delegates to the Lancashire and Claeshire Union of Conservative Associations. _ _ .

Mr. Bsrron moved the following resolution That this the annual general meeting of the Newton Division Conservative Association, desires to express its sincere and unabated confidence in the wise and successful policy of Lord Salisbury and his colleagues in South Af.ica and thanks them for their past untiring efforts to provide for freedom and good government for all races in the country and for upholding and preserving the dignity and integrity of the British Empire, afar! further I tegs to thank them for the beneficial legialttion passed since their acc.ssion to power." Mr. Wyndham Smith, who secended, remarked that the Government were not fighting, as some persons seemed to imagine, the battle of the capitalists in S outh Africa, but they were struggling to maintain tee supra- ' macy of the British Empire. Colonel Pilkingten, M.P., supported the resolution. He said that since their meeting of a year ago the pettiest scene had changed in a wonderful way. He did net know anyone who thought last April that the country would be engaged in a great war at the present time. The Boers had been giving trouble, but very few persons —perhaps only Lord Salisbury and Mr. Chamberlain— theught that it would come to so serious a crisis as it had done. The Boers had been treated like spoiled chil- dren, they had been given everything they asked for, through the magnanimity of the British Empire. The opinion throughout the British Empire was strong and eathuaiastic that this war was a rightful war, and that ft must be carried through to the end. (Hear, boar) He thought that the greatest proof the war was a right- ful war was to be foend in the action of our celoaies. The colonies had responded nobly to the call of the mother country, and in that the British people had much to be thankful for. (Hear. hear.) The colonies had suppled an army of 30,900 fight- ing men. Who would have thought twelve months ago that they would hate done so well? The whole conduct of the war, the transport of the troops, and the bravery of the men at the front, were matters which Englishmen bad a good right to be proud of. (Hear, hear.) Eng- lishmen, Irishmen, Scotchmen, Welshmen, Australians, New Zealandersoried with each other in acts of courage and bravery on the battle field in defence of the Empire. (Hear, hear.) Under such circumstances could anyone doubt as to whet the result of the war would be? But they eould not forget that Great Britain had many enemies, and that she may have to stand alone in battle array against the foe. In order to prepare for such an eventuality the army must be reorganised, and every man must be able to use a gun in defence of his country in case of necessity. This war had taugnt us many les- sons which he hoped would have the effect of preparing the country in her own defence. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the settlement of the South African R onsbOea after the war they all felt that there could be but one settlement—their incorporation into the British Empire under the supremacy of Caueen Victoria, so that there should never again be any possibility at their rebellioa. (H' ear hear.) It would be for the Unionist Government to do that work. He could not lay the blame for the state of the Transvaal and its wonderful military equ7p- resent at the ds,or of any one of the parties in this coun- try. Both parties were to blame in the past, although the greater portion of the blame should be laid against the Liberal Government, which in 1981 neglected te settle the question for ever. It was therefore an advan- tage to have Lord Selisbury'e Government in power at preseat, and he felt sure that they would come to a setteament which would be permanent, and beneficial to the Empire at large. (Hear. hear.) Lord Newton, supporting the resolution,said he looked upon the war as a hateful nec-ssity. Tree en )rinous losses which Great Britain had already suffered in men and moray would hardly be atoned for by the results The direct reselt of the war would, in his opinion, be In ost distinctly inadequate. But it was a war which it was i -epossible to avoid. The plain truth was that Mr. Rhodes, Dr. Jameson, and the rest of that craw did their best to spoil England's case. It was plain to everybody that the Boers and their Dutch sympathisers had been preparing for a long time to turn the British out of South Africa, and if they had waited a little bit longer they would have succeeded in their purpose. We had had a narrow escape. And to what did we owe the relief of those towns that had coarly fallen ? We did not owe it to persons in authority : we owed it almost entirely to the stubborn tenacity of the British soldier— (cheers) —and statesmanship and generalship had vary much less to de with success than had the courage of the soldier. (Hear, hear.) The first lesson which the British people had learnt from the war was that they were almost universally detested. The only countries in Europe that had any sympathy with Great Britain were the smaller States, such as Greece, Norway, and,perhaps Denmark ; and although we valued their sympathy, it was never likely to take practical or tangible form ; and if we took America we could find but very few symptoms of our case being regarded with impartiality. England was charged with a desire to grab territory in the in- terests of the millionaires. That was absurd. although Mr. Rhodes and his friends had done their best to substantiate the charge. He could not account for the feeling of universal detesta- tion with which England was regarded unless it was that the ill-feeling had been prompted by jealousy because of our wealth and power. He was inclined to think that the ill-feeling was in a great nensure due to Englishmen's own conduct. It was due to the sentimental blundering that we indulged in. We were fend lof interfering In other people's affairs,and that interference was resented by parties who refused to be- lieve in our disinterested motives. At any rat., one of the clear lessons of this war was that we had very few friends, and that we must look upon the future in quite a different manner to that in which we regarded the past. He would go so far as to say that we owed our immunity from the intervention of another Power in the war to the fact that England had got the most powerful nest in the world. (Hear, hear). A Liberal statesman had said that no nation in Europe was prepared to risk its fleet against that of England. He thought that was the truth, and if it was so then the thanks for so strong a fleet were dam to a Conservative Government. (Applause.) For that reason alone the Government were entitled to support, even if some !relple were not satis- fied with them in other matters. The second lesson to be learnt from the war was an equally disagreeable one. We had learnt that in a military sense we were inefficient ; that our military system was inadequate. In order to subdue two small petty Republics we were obliged to employ our whole militay strength, and besides that, to summon our Colonies to our assistance. But he could imagine a worse condition of things. He could imaeine our being involved in other parts of the world as well—with difficulties in Afghanis- tan, in China, Persia,in the Mediterrarean.and Ashantee. Where should we he eupposing there were troubles with these countries? He supposed a bold effart would be made to grapple with our military system, and to place our home defence on a firm basis ; and that it would have been the duty of the Government to consult with the responsible chiefs of the Opposition—if there were such people—(laughter) —end to agree upon a scheme of defence which would secure the safety of the courstree Personally ho regretted that the opportunity had not been taken advantage of, and he also regretted that. the Government had unequivocally rejected every preposal in the nature of compulsion for military service for this country. Be saw no hardship in com- pulsory service. Where was the hardship in 'tying that a man should protect his own home? Every European nation did it, and why Englishmen should not do it passed his comprehension. Lord Salis- bury had said thee the youth of the country were going abroad to escape conscription. Nobody proposed con- scription in the form in which it was understood in great 'military nations. The means proposed was that every young man should do a few months' training in the course of his life for the purpose of being able to protect his own home. (Hear' hear.) To say that such a system as that would upset tise whole social fabric was nonsense. It was not fair that 99 per cent, of the citizens of the country should be protected at the expense of the other 1 per cent. A moral obligation rested epon every citizen to do something for the defence of his country. A small propottion acted up to that moral obliga- tion. and what was proposed was that that obligation should he extended. Lancashire had done its part recently, and be hoped the pressure would be kept up. Would the military enthusiasm of the past few months continue after the close of the war? For his own part he did not believe that that enthusiasm would continue. The course they were pursuing was an absurdity. They clamoured for extension of the Em- pire, but they absolutely refused to countenance any scheme upon which the home defence of the country could be put on a permanent basis. The weak point in the voluntary system was that if too severe a standard of efficiency was exacted the voluetary system would disappear altogether. One alternative was that the compulsory system should be adopted ; • the other was that the soldier in the regular army should be paid the same wages as he could obtain in trade. (Hear, hear.) Be should like to see the face of the Chancellor of the Exchequer if such a proposal as the latter were placed before him. But one of these alternatives would have to be adopted,and the sooner the better. One of the serious problems which the country would have to face

was that of the results of the settlement in South Africa The colonies would exprct that some return should be made to them for their sacrifices. For his part he thought they would insist upon some commercial advantages which might entirely revolutionise our tariff. It seemed to him that to talk of magnanimity and generosity in dealing with the 'Transvaal and the Orange Free State was siogular:y out of place. (Hear, hear.) The Boers had been trusted and tried before, and they had been found wanting. Millions of money had been spent in order to make—what ?—a display of magnanimity and generosity ? No, this time the settlement should he made in our interest, and he felt convincEd that the corn monsense of this country would be marked less by ma2nanirnity anu generosity than by justice and prud- ence and self-interest, and above all by permanence. (Applause.) The resolution was then put from the chair, and was declared carried untnimoualy. Thanks were 'given to Colonel Pilkington for his ad- dre•is, and t 3 the noble chairman for his conduct of the proceedings.

CIVIELTY TO A HORSE.—William Stanway was charge 1 with illtreating a hlrse by causing it to be worked whilst in an unfit state at Haydock on the 13th Atpr.l ; Alfred Vsrly was summoned for working the same.—They pleased not gulity.—lnspector Jonas. R.S.P.O A., said he saw the defendant Vsrly in charge of a grey mare attached to a cart laden with salt. He noticed it was very lam- and stopped it On making an examination of the animal be found it to be aged and in a poor condition. He saw Stanway and he said he was not aware that the horse was unit to work.—Another Insoeator stated that the animal was completely worn out.—The defendant Stanway said he had only just bohcht ths animal and was not aware that there was anything the matter with it. Ho gave £4 for IL—The Chairman: What is it doing now ?—Stanway: I have sold it I don't know what it is doing —The Clerk : How much did you get for it P—Stanway : 12s.—Stanway was tined 10s and costs and Varly was ordered to pay 5s and hosts.

TRESPASSING IN &WWII OE GAME.—David Critchley, Thomas Maudeley, and James Shaw were summoned for trespassing on land in the occupation of Lord Newton in search of conies on the 18th of April.—Shaw did not appear and the other defendants pleaded guilty.—Mr ki. J. Longton prosecuted, and stated that at 3 o'clock on the date in ques- tion the defendants were seen in a wood called " The Grange." They had two dogs with them and appeared to be searching for game. There were rabbits and other game in the wood.—George William Sale stated that he saw the defendants enter the wood accompanied by two dogs. They extenined a place which was fr.,quented by rabbits.—The defendants. who were well know' characters to the police, were fined 20s and costs each.

div.head: ALLEGED HOUSEE3KEAKING AND ASSAULT AT OITTON.
div.p: ALLEGED HOUSEE3KEAKING AND ASSAULT AT OITTON.

At the Widnes Police C9urt,on Monday morning,h.fore the Mayor (Alderman G. I. Neil) and Alderman Ware- ing, a young man named Patrick Flaughey was charged with breaking aril entering the dwelling-house. 2, Greenall's-cottages, Ditton, at 3 a.m, on the 15th inst. Tao prn,eeutrix, Annie G:egory sts.ted that the pri- soner had been lodging at the house of her mother for a considerable thee. He had been on friendly terms with her husband, and had often visited their house. On the 14.311 her husband left honio at 5 p.m. to go to his work. She retired to bed at 11 4s, but before doing so she bolted the back door and locked the front. About three o'clock she was awakened by the prisoner. Thinking it was her husband, she asked what brought him horn 6 so sqpn. He replied, "It is not Sam, Annie; it's me " Prisoner, she alleged, assaul-

ted her, and she screamed and attempted to get away. She got up and throw an earthenware ornatnent at the man. He said if she made a noise and brought the neighbours around he would strangle her. Witness knocked on the wall to awaken her neighbours, but no one answered. Prisoner then ran downstairs. At the time she had the lamp bdrsing. After the prisoner had left she went to her mother's and informed her of the affair. When her husband returned they went to their house to ascertain, if posisible, how the man had gained admittance. On an examination of the back bedroom they found the window taken out and leaning against the wall on the floor. They went into the yard, and found a ladder whiet did not belong to them. ALyone getting into the bedroom wou:d regniie a 14d ier.—ln re-ply to prisoner witness said that he came to her how() on Saturday afternoon at 2.30 with her husband. They had two quarts of beer. He was in the house on Good Friday evening, aed he then had had drink. He fell asleep on the chair, leaving at 10 30. Sae was not drunk on Friday eveninz, and she remembered everything. The back door was opm when she came downstairs nu Sun- day morninz, Dr. C Hu' &linson spoke to examining the woman and finding bruises on her body. When asked if he had anything to say, prisoner replied that he had not. Flo was co omitted to toe ASSiZ'!ti for trial, bail Wing allowed, himself in £4O, and tw%) sure- ties of £25 each,

Cheshire Lines Workmen's Provident Society. The 25th annual meeting of the Cheshire Linea Platelayers and Workmen's Provident Society, which consists of the workmen employed in the Engineer's Department of the Cheshire Lines Rail- way, was held at the work', Battersby-lane, War- rington on Thursday. In the unavoidable absence of the Chief Engineer Mr. W C Scott, C.E., the chair was taken by Mr Robert Slater,district inspec- tor and the meeting was largely attended by officials end delegates from Lancashire and Cheshire. The Secretary submitted the annual report,which stated that the number of members was 1265. A large sum had been expended in aid of 316 sick members who had received assistance from the funds of the Society and 29 death claims had else been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed, Mr Thomas Pratt was re-elected secretary for the ensuing year and Messrs. George Walker and Robert Jones were elected auditors. PADGATE. Parish Council. The annual meeting of the Padget° Parish Council was held in the schoolroo:n on Friday night. There wens present Messrs George Walker, Henry Thornton, G Mather, R Denham G Hatton, JJ. Harrington. T H Grainger and F Wright (clerk). riLecriorrs. Mr H Thornton proposed the re-election of Mr George Walker as chairman for the ensuing year. Mr. Harrington seconded. Mr. G. Mather -was proposed, but on a vote being taken only the proposer (Mr. Denham) and seconder (Mr. Hatton) voted in favour of the amendment. Mr. Walker was therefore re-elected, and briefly returned thanks for the honour conferred upon him. On the motion of Mr. Harrington seconded by Mr. Grainger,Mr. Thornton was uaanimously re-elected vice- chairman. Mr. Thornton in responding referred to the expen- diture of money by the Rural District Council. He said that Mr. Thompson always stated in open meetings of the Rural District Council that every parish bad its own money expended but it hid come out that this was not so. The Council had been expending money where they preferred to do so. This was rather an important mat- , ter to that and other parishes because other parishes were dissatisfied: It was an uphill task to fight against these things and it didL not make a man popular in that sense but so long as he represented the joint parishes he should struggle for the interests of the parishes. (Hear, hear.) That was what he had endeavoured to do all along, and he thought it was a very important matter. OVERSEERS. Messrs Walker. Harrington and Hattm were appointed overseers. Mr Wright was re-Aected assistantoverver and clerk. Mr El Wright was elec'ed treasurer. DATES OF MEETINGS. It was decided that the qu irterly meetings should be held on the Friday following the 15th of the usual quarter months. FINANCE COMMITTEE. The Chairman, Mr. Denham and Mr. Grainger were re-elected to form the ab)ve committee. This concluded the meeting. Action against a Warrington Firm. In the Nisi Prins Court at the Manchester Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice Phillimoro and a special jury, a tube welder named Joseph Cooksey, claimed damages for broach of agreement from Messrs. Monks, Mall and Co,,Limited,Warring- ton. Mr. Pickford, Q C., and Mr. Mansfield were for the plaintiff, Mr. Taylor, Q.C., and Mr. Langdon for the def,.ndants. The plaintiff was engaged by the defendants for four years as a tube welder, and it was admitted that he was dismissed. The plaintiff employed other servants, who were known as a "sat," and who worked under his direction and were paid by him. The defendants alleged that the plaintiff had not given his personal attendance at the works as he ought to have done, that he was often abrent,and when there on some occasions was in a state of intoxication. On the other hand it was contended that the latter charges were after- thoughts, and that with regard to attendance the plaintiff wal not under contract to be present in given hours, but had contracted te:, do the welding. lie urged, in fact, that he was in a position of a contractor; the defendants held that he was in that of a servan.t.—The evidence for the plaintiff was concluded and the case opened for the defendants, when the jury intimated that they were unani- naously in favour of a verdict for the defendants. Judgment was given accordingly.
